intro: Displayed with the Cape York Exhibition is the lovely Cape York Lily, Curcuma australasica, a member of the ginger family. The large, pleated leaves sheathe the clusters of rosy pink flowers which change to green on ageing. The tuberous stock was roasted and eaten by Aborigines.

intro: This walk is to discover the winter flowering plants in the Rock Garden. The large rocks in the Rock Garden act as a source of heat, absorbing during the day and radiating slowly at night. The soil mixes in the different beds provide suitable growing conditions for a range of special plants.
p: Crowea `Festival' [Section 15C] is a neat, rounded shrub covered, in profusion, with bright pink star-like flowers which continue for a long period.

Along the Banks Walk, Eriostemon angustifolia [Section 210] is a small plant dotted with small star flowers and Phebalium nottii [Section 210] is a small, open plant showing the first of many dark centred, pink flowers.

Along the Banks Walk, Eriostemon angustifolia [Section 210] is a small plant dotted with small star flowers and Phebalium nottii [Section 210] is a small, open plant showing the first of many dark centred, pink flowers.
Grevillea alpina `Gold Rush' [Section 174] is quite dense and is well illuminated with its gold flowers.
At the end of the cafe building, Micromyrtus ciliata [Section 12], is a small plant with spreading branches covered with red buds just thinking of bursting into tiny white flowers.
Looking down to the Banks Centre, Banksia `Giant Candles' [Section 143] stands erect with its long golden cylindrical flower spikes reaching for the sky.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
More brilliant are the shorter flower spikes of Banksia ericifolia var. ericifolia [Section 143].
Banksia robur [Section 181], Swamp Banksia, seen beside the small brook, has large, leathery leaves.
Nearby is Grevillea diminuta [Section 178] which reveals its rust coloured flowers in pendulous clusters.
They include Banksia spinulosa var. collina [Section 28] with pale yellow flower spikes.
Here also is Banksia oblongifolia [Section 27] which has small flower spikes of varying shades of green.
Walk under the large, arching branches of Eucalyptus baeuerlenii [Section 28] which provides many lacy, cream flowers with nectar for the discerning birds.
As yet small, Grevillea victoriae [Section 27], Royal Grevillea, bears orange-red pendent flowers clusters.
In this area of hakeas, Hakea cristata [Section 23] is quite spectacular with small clusters of white flowers along its branches.
Hakea sericea [Section 21, 20] is long and lanky, with branches laden with fruits.
Hakea bakeriana [Section 21] is more rounded, with longer needle-like leaves and with large, pink flower clusters on old wood, mostly behind the foliage.
Edging the main path is a small plant, Guichenotia macrantha [Section 4] with hairy foliage and hairy bell shaped, mauve flowers.
The miniature Banksia `Birthday Candles' [Section 15] in front of the water-fall is alight with a red tinted, gold flower spikes ...
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)

intro: As the newly constructed Main Path is now complete, this walk will follow its course. Between the large rocks at the beginning of the walk the grey, almost white, foliage of some plants is most apparent. Particularly note Leucophyta brownii [Section 210] with its long branches extending along the gr
p: Particularly note Leucophyta brownii [Section 210] with its long branches extending along the ground.
Out into the warm wintery sun, see Banksia aemula [Section 16] which is quite a dense shrub with serrated leaves and cream-coloured cylindrical flower spikes.
Crowea `Festival' [Section 16] is neat and rounded with terminal red branches and pink star flowers.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Take time, here to discover the beauties throughout the Rockery area, but first, in front of the waterfall, marvel at the miniature Banksia `Birthday Candles' [Section 15].
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)

Sharing the garden bed is Crowea exalata [Section 15], a prostrate form bearing small pink star flowers and Correa reflexa `Carpenters Rock' [Section 15], a small, open plant decorated with red tubular flowers with yellow tips.

Sharing the garden bed is Crowea exalata [Section 15], a prostrate form bearing small pink star flowers and Correa reflexa `Carpenters Rock' [Section 15], a small, open plant decorated with red tubular flowers with yellow tips.
Pass by an area of hakeas, spotting, in the background, Hakea sericea [Section 20] with a cover of tiny pink lacy flowers over a tall shrub with an abundance of dark fruits.
Flannel Flowers, Actinotus helianthi [Section 191], with velvety white, daisy-like flowers on long stalks continue to flower.
Banksia spinulosa var. spinulosa [Section 191] bears golden cylindrical flower spikes, on one shrub ribbed with dark styles, on another with red styles.
Platysace lanceolata [Section 191] is low and dense with clusters of tiny white flowers dotted over the dark green foliage.
Over the rock wall in front of the seat, see Grevillea victoriae [Section 191] with orange red pendent flowers on a still small shrub.
Banksia integrifolia var. integrifolia [Section 30] is a tall shrub with short lemon flower spikes mingling with silver-backed foliage.
And at the corner of the cafe building, Correa reflexa `Maroonda Tricolour' [Section 240] reveals its delightful array of tubular flowers coloured red, yellow and green.
So, across the bridge Crowea saligna [Section 174] with bright, waxy pink flowers and waxy, light green leaves covering this small plant is the selected prize to end the Main Path walk.

intro: This walk will follow the Main Path, commencing at the large rocks along Banks Walk. Between these rocks, the soft grey-white foliage of Leucophyta brownii [Section 210] is prominent. Grevillea `Poorinda Tranquility' [Section 210] is a small shrub dotted with attractive peach coloured flowers. Follo
p: Between these rocks, the soft grey-white foliage of Leucophyta brownii [Section 210] is prominent.
Grevillea `Poorinda Tranquility' [Section 210] is a small shrub dotted with attractive peach coloured flowers.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)

See such beauties as the Rough Treefern, Cyathea australis [Section 148] with large fronds radiating from the trunk apex and the Hoop Pine, Araucaria cunninghamii [Section 64], with tall, straight, dark trunk and systemmatically arranged branches.

See such beauties as the Rough Treefern, Cyathea australis [Section 148] with large fronds radiating from the trunk apex and the Hoop Pine, Araucaria cunninghamii [Section 64], with tall, straight, dark trunk and systemmatically arranged branches.
See, in front of the waterfall, the miniature Banksia `Birthday Candles' [Section 15], each plant with its yellow, cylindrical flower spike tinged with red styles.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
A prostrate form of Crowea exalata [Section 15] nearby continues to produce small, pink star flowers.
Guichenotia macrantha [Section 4] is a small plant adorned with interesting bell-like pink flowers.
The area of hakeas includes Hakea bakeriana [Section 20].
Hakea sericea [Section 20] is a large, many branched shrub with a covering of pale pink lacy flowers.
The next area is that of the Sydney Region Flora where Banksia spinulosa var. spinulosa [Section 191] continues to bear golden flower spikes.

Grevillea miqueliana [Section 26] is a shrub of medium size dotted with soft pink flowers and nearby Grevillea aspleniifolia [Section 26], with short trunk and long lateral branches, is worth admiring because of its unique design.

Grevillea miqueliana [Section 26] is a shrub of medium size dotted with soft pink flowers and nearby Grevillea aspleniifolia [Section 26], with short trunk and long lateral branches, is worth admiring because of its unique design.
Grevillea victoriae [Section 25] is as yet small and open and laden with deep rust-red spider-like flowers.
Banksia integrifolia var. integrifolia [Section 30] stands tall with silver-backed leaves and small, lemon flower spikes.
Banksia ericifolia var. ericifolia [Section 30] glows with longer, golden flower spikes.
See the Grass Tree, Xanthorrhoea glauca subsp. glauca [Section 8] with brown skirt and swirling green top.

intro: This walk will discover winter flowering plants not damaged by recent heavy frosts in the Rock Garden. The large rocks in this area act as a source of heat, absorbed during the day and radiated slowly after dark. The soil mixes in the different beds supply suitable growing conditions for a range of
p: Crowea `Festival' [Section 15C] is a neat, dense, long-flowering shrub still with numerous deep pink star-like flowers.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Correa `Ivory Bells' [Section 15D] is another shrub which flowers for a long time.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Further back, the Grass Tree, Xanthorrhoea johnsonii [Section 15D] is always an eyecatcher because of its crop of long, twirling grass-like leaves.
The brilliant yellow straw flower heads of Bracteantha species [Section 15D] can be seen in various areas.
Homoranthus darwinioides [Section 15F] is a low, spreading plant with foliage coloured mauve-grey and tiny pendulous flowers, once yellow, now reddening as they age.
Around the corner find Guichenotia macrantha [Sections 15F and 4] which has velvety pink bell-like flowers along an upright stem.
Phebalium lamprophyllum [Section 15N] has an attractive covering of clusters of deep red buds and is already showing a few tiny white flowers.
Melichrus adpressus [Section 15K] is not flowering but is quite interesting for this dwarf shrub has branches densely packed with short, green leaves.
Melichrus urceolatus [Section 15K] is low and spreading and is dotted with tiny, lemon tubular flowers.
Dryandra squarrosa [Section 15P] is a tall, many branched shrub which continues to produce many yellow flower-heads scattered among the fine toothed leaves.
Grevillea maxwellii [Section 15P], a semi-prostrate, spreading plant has deep red grape-like clusters of flowers which are almost concealed by the much divided leaves.
Hardenbergia violacea `Mini Haha' [Section 15S] is upright, dense and just exploding with deep purple pea flowers.
Nearby Leucophyta brownii `Cape le Grand' [Section 15S] is an interesting dwarf plant with wiry silvery stems.

Correa pulchella [Section 15S] continues to bear soft pink, tubular flowers, and, in front of the waterfall, Correa reflexa `Carpenters Rock' [Section 15] is resplendent with small red, tubular flowers tipped with yellow.

Correa pulchella [Section 15S] continues to bear soft pink, tubular flowers, and, in front of the waterfall, Correa reflexa `Carpenters Rock' [Section 15] is resplendent with small red, tubular flowers tipped with yellow.

intro: Banksias continue to flower, wattles and grevilleas are seen to be bursting into flower and many other plants are still awaiting the warmer spring climate. This walk will include mostly the first three.
p: View the bright red trumpet-shaped flowers of Rhododendron lactum x lochiae; the Kangaroo Paw, Anigozanthos manglesii with unbranched, woolly maroon stems and red and green flowers and Mirbelia speciosa subsp.

In the Display Garden along Banks Walk, Grevillea alpina `Gold Rush' [Section 174] is dotted with bright yellow flowers and Grevillea `Scarlet Sprite' [Section 174] sparkles with red flowers.
In the Display Garden along Banks Walk, Grevillea alpina `Gold Rush' [Section 174] is dotted with bright yellow flowers and Grevillea `Scarlet Sprite' [Section 174] sparkles with red flowers.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Follow the main path and find Queensland Silver Wattle, Acacia podalyriifolia [Section 119], a tall shrub with grey green foliage ablaze with golden yellow, fluffy flower balls.
Nearby, Micromyrtus ciliata [Section 10] is a low, arching plant covered with red buds, now exploding into tiny white flowers.
Branch off at Banksia spinulosa var. collina [Section 28], a medium, rounded shrub bearing long, lemon flower-spikes with fine, needle foliage.
Nearby is Banksia oblongifolia [Section 27] with deep green flower-spikes.
A prostrate form of Grevillea lanigera [Section 27] is quite dense with a covering of red flowers.
Sit awhile and admire Banksia ericifolia var. ericifolia [Section 28], of medium size and always with tall, dazzling, golden flower-spikes.
Nearby Banksia occidentalis [Section 28] with tall, mottled trunks has eye-catching flower spikes of lemon accentuated with red, hooked styles.
Compare a hybrid form of Grevillea juniperina [Section 27] and Grevillea rosmarinifolia [Section 27].
Compare a hybrid form of Grevillea juniperina [Section 27] and Grevillea rosmarinifolia [Section 27].
Banksia integrifolia var. compar [Section 27] is a tall, graceful shrub with lemon flower spikes, dotted with grey, set among the smooth, shiny, silver-backed leaves.
Over the road, set among the greenery, the splash of brilliant yellow flowers is that of the Cootamundra Wattle, Acacia baileyana [Section 192] ...

intro: Spring is almost here and our lovely city is already glowing with the golden wattles. In the Gardens, many wattles are still in bud while some are bursting into flower. Others are already ablaze of golden glory, some of which will be included, as well as other flowers, on this walk.
p: Firstly, in the pots outside the Visitor Centre door, see the brilliant red flower-heads of Grevillea brachystylis.
In another pot, a small plant, Lechenaultia formosa bears bright orange flowers.
Outside the main gates Acacia flexifolia bears, in profusion, pale yellow globular flower head on small, dense shrubs.

Draped over the retaining walls in the carpark, Acacia cultriformis `Austraflora Cascade' [Section 226] and Acacia baileyana [Section 226] both prostrate plants, are showing the first of their golden flowers.

Draped over the retaining walls in the carpark, Acacia cultriformis `Austraflora Cascade' [Section 226] and Acacia baileyana [Section 226] both prostrate plants, are showing the first of their golden flowers.
At the bus stop, Acacia phasmoides [Section 174] is of medium size with open branches bearing narrow, sickle-shaped phyllodes (modified leaves) and yellow rod-shaped flowers.
Acacia kybeanensis [Section 182] Kybean Wattle, has fluffy yellow flower-balls in clusters among the grey-green foliage.
Queensland Silver Wattle, Acacia podalyriifolia [Section 126, 119] is a tall shrub with grey-green foliage ablaze with golden yellow, fluffy flower balls.
Grevillea `Scarlet Sprite' [Section 119] is a small plant with cheery red spider-like flowers mingling with the fine foliage.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Acacia baileyana `Purpurea' [Section 3] is another eye-catcher for its lovely arching golden covered branches are tipped with purple coloured leaves.
Acacia boormanii [Section 3,2] Snowy River Wattle, is of medium size with fine foliage mixed with soft yellow, well perfumed flowers.
Banksia spinulosa var. spinulosa [Section 37] is a dense, medium sized shrub showing tall, cylindrical deep gold flower-spikes which are ribbed with dark styles.
Banksia plagiocarpa [Section 37] is an open shrub with small, unique coloured mauve-grey flower-spikes.
Above the stairs, the green flowering Banksia oblongifolia [Section 37c] can be seen, beside which is Grevillea floribunda [Section 37c] with lovely dangling rust coloured spider-like flowers.
Above the stairs, the green flowering Banksia oblongifolia [Section 37c] can be seen, beside which is Grevillea floribunda [Section 37c] with lovely dangling rust coloured spider-like flowers.

intro: This walk will follow the Main Path from which the golden glow of wattles can be seen in most areas. Snowy River Wattle, Acacia boormanii [Section 210] is now covered with perfumed, fluffy yellow flower clusters. Between the rocks, see Adenanthos detmoldii [Section 210], a small plant with spirally
p: Snowy River Wattle, Acacia boormanii [Section 210] is now covered with perfumed, fluffy yellow flower clusters.
Between the rocks, see Adenanthos detmoldii [Section 210], a small plant with spirally arranged tiny leaves and slim, tubular yellow flowers along the branches.
Opposite is Thryptomene saxicola `Pink Lace' [Section 210] with arching branches bearing tiny pink flowers.
Banksia spinulosa var. spinulosa [Section 210] is of medium size alight with upright, golden flower spikes which are ribbed with dark styles.
Close to the path is Hardenbergia violacea `Mini Haha' [Section 15] which is laden with purple pea flowers on this upright shrub.
Nearby is Lechenaultia formosa [Section 15], a small plant with orange flowers, and Lechenaultia `Scarlet O'Hara' [Section 15] also with brilliantly coloured flowers.
Nearby is Lechenaultia formosa [Section 15], a small plant with orange flowers, and Lechenaultia `Scarlet O'Hara' [Section 15] also with brilliantly coloured flowers.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Guichenotia macrantha [Section 4] is a small plant having showy pink bell-shaped flowers.
In this area of hakeas, see Hakea bakeriana [Section 20] which continues to bear large clusters of pink flowers attached to the old wood behind the foliage.
Hakea purpurea [Section 20] is a rather lanky shrub beautified with cherry-coloured flowers.
Across the road are wattles which include a prostrate form of the Cootamundra Wattle, Acacia baileyana [Section 18], with radiating branches of golden flower balls.
Hibbertia saligna [Section 191] has many buds exploding into bold yellow flowers.
Edging the path, Sowerbaea juncea [Section 191] is small with rush-like leaves and dark purple buds already opening on upright purple-tinted stems.
Mirbelia speciosa [Section 191], also very small, has deep purple pea flowers along the upright stems.
Grevillea miqueliana [Section 26] is of medium size and bears pink spider-like flowers.
Grevillea paniculata [Section 26] is quite open and covered with lemon, perfumed flowers.
Across the road Grevillea victoriae [Section 25] is laden with deep rust-red spider-like flowers.
See the dazzling golden flower spikes of Banksia ericifolia var. ericifolia [Section 30] then hopefully, time for a tasty nibble with coffee at the cafe.

intro: Wattles continue to highlight our fine city and these Gardens with glowing yellow flowers. This walk is close to the Visitor Centre where many wattles can be seen. The colourful plants outside the doors include Thryptomene calycina `Coral Lace' with tiny coral-coloured flowers crowded over the grace
p: The colourful plants outside the doors include Thryptomene calycina `Coral Lace' with tiny coral-coloured flowers crowded over the graceful terminal branches.
Nearby Thryptomene calycina `Ivory Lace' is equally as attractive.
Acacia covenyi [Section 225] commonly called Blue Bush because of its blue-green foliage which shares the outer branches with fluffy, golden flower balls.
Draped over the retaining walls of the newer car park, the golden flowers of Cootamundra Wattle, Acacia baileyana [Section 227], are quite dazzling.
Along the upper retaining wall, Acacia cultriformis `Austraflora Cascade' [Section 226] is covered with buds which are beginning to explode into golden flower balls.
Grevillea dimorpha [Section 226] is a low, open shrub brilliant with bright red flowers clustered along its branches.
Australia's floral emblem, Acacia pycnantha [Section 224], with shiny sickle-shaped foliage is laden with buds now bursting ito large golden flower balls.
At its base Grevillea `Scarlet Sprite' [Section 224], a low, neat, rounded shrub, is illuminated with lovely red spider-like flowers.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Nearby Correa reflexa var. reflexa [Section 224] reveals its yellow-tipped red tubular flowers pendent from sparse branches.
In front of the building, Grevillea diminuta [Section 222] is a low, dense shrub bearing interesting rust-red flowers in pendulous clusters, almost hidden by the dark green foliage.
Opposite Westringia crassifolia [Section 221,174] is a small and open plant dotted with delicate mauve flowers.

Nearby is Eucalyptus caesia subsp. magna [Section 221], its long arching trunk with bark cracking and peeling, its silver branches falling to ground level and supporting the large, splendid deep pink, dotted yellow flowers ...
Over the road in the Grassy Woodlands area Hardenbergia violacea [Section 175] with deep purple pea flowers, climbs over and beautifies surrounding shrubs.
Pomaderris intermedia [Section 175] has large heads of yellow flowers on tall, open branches.
Acacia genistifolia [Section 175] is of medium size with needle-like foliage and generously covered with large, cream flower balls.
Halfway up the stairs Zieria sp.O [Section 221] has a profusion of tiny pink flower clusters which blend with the green-grey foliage.

intro: On leaving the Visitor Centre turn right, and on the left-hand side, Hardenbergia violacea [Section 210] can be seen in full bloom with its deep purple pea flowers. Next to it is Acacia boormanii [Section 210], commonly known as the Snowy River Wattle, a rounded shrub which is found naturally in Vic
p: On leaving the Visitor Centre turn right, and on the left-hand side, Hardenbergia violacea [Section 210] can be seen in full bloom with its deep purple pea flowers.
Next to it is Acacia boormanii [Section 210], commonly known as the Snowy River Wattle, a rounded shrub which is found naturally in Victoria and New South Wales.
To the right, Epacris longiflora [Section 174] displays its white tubular flowers in pendent rows along stiff wiry stems.
Further down is Templetonia retusa [Section 174], look at the large orange/red pea flowers.
Another Western Australian plant in flower is Brachysema celsianum [Section 110], bright cherry red pea flowers contrasted against blue-green foliage.
In the Rockery Tetratheca ciliata [Section 15D], to the right of the waterfall, is showing its delicate white bell-like flowers which are hanging down hiding their black centres.
Continue along the main path, crossing the road and there to the left is Acacia phasmoides [Section 19] with gold flower rods and long, narrow curving leaves.
On entering, just to the right is Acacia myrtifolia [Section 191], a rounded bush with attractive red-tinged foliage and creamy-lemon flower heads.
Further along the path to the left is Epacris sp. aff. impressa [Section 191], with red tubular flowers which are in profusion now and are produced throughout the year.
Leucopogon muticus [Section 191] is about to burst forth with its tiny urn-like white flowers.

At the intersection of the path and road on the right side is Acacia gordonii [Section 191], a small spreading shrub with crowded foliage almost hidden by brilliant, electric golden yellow flower balls.
Continue on to see Hakea propinqua [Section 191] with its tight little curly yellow flowers perched in the axils of the leaves; notice too the enormous woody fruits.
At the head of the gully, Epacris microphylla [Section 191] is in full bloom with white starry flowers which are present most of the year.
Last but not least, looking towards the Eucalypt Lawn, is Grevillea aspleniifolia [Section 191], a large spreading shrub with long thin leaves and pink toothbrush flowers.

intro: This week's walk will be along the new Main Path.
p: At the beginning of the main path on the left is Epacris impressa `Cranbourne Bells' [Section 212] with its pendent, white, tubular flowers along the stem.
Next door is Pimelea spectabilis [Section 212], a Western Australian plant.
Baeckea ramosissima `Pink Gem' [Section 212] is a spreading shrub, which has delicate magenta pink petals with crimson centres.
Another Epacris in flower is Epacris hamiltonii [Section 212], flushes of white flowers clustered together on the stem.
Thryptomene saxicola `Pink Lace' [Section 212] has small pink flowers.
On entering the Rainforest, on your left is Zieria arborescens [Section 148b], with small white delicate four-petalled flowers and a slight aromatic perfume.
Continue along the board walk, just opposite two seats is Blackwood, Acacia melanoxylon [Section 148], in flower.
Citriobatus pauciflorus [Section 65], common in rainforests of NSW and Queensland has bright orange fruits.
Soft Treeferns, Dicksonia antarctica [Section 65a] dominate throughout the gully as an understorey, the decorative young fronds beginning to uncurl are beautiful to see.
Just before the Rockery is Banksia aemula [Section 16] with its old flower heads and serrated leaves.

intro: To continue with last week's walk along the new Main Path, we will start at the Rockery. Telopea speciosissima `Wirrimbirra White' [Section 15d] has burst forth with its majestic cream white flowers. Further along the path Tetratheca ciliata [Section 15] found in New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania
p: Telopea speciosissima `Wirrimbirra White' [Section 15d] has burst forth with its majestic cream white flowers.
Further along the path Tetratheca ciliata [Section 15] found in New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania and South Australia is showing its white flower bells in profusion.
Hakea bakeriana [Section 20], in the Proteaceae Section, has enormous woody fruits and on the stems can be seen large pink spider flowers.
To the left nearby is Hakea purpurea [Section 20], with crimson red spider flowers amongst sharp spiky foliage.
In particular notice Acacia cognata [Section 19] with its graceful weeping stems, long thin foliage and lemon coloured flowers.
Acacia fimbriata [Section 18] is another fine example, the boughs are sweeping the ground weighed down with its golden flowers.
On entering the Eucalypt Lawn look at the different textures of the bark, in particular Eucalyptus eximia [Section 19a], its papery patterned bark of ochres and greys is lovely to touch.
In the Sydney Region Flora there is Banksia serrata [Section 191] covered in old flower cones with their velvety prominent fruits.
Sowerbaea juncea [Section 191] lining the path on the right hand side has pretty clusters of fragile mauve flowers.
The boronias are in flower, Boronia deanei [Section 191] has delicate four-petalled pink flowers.
Pomaderris ferruginea [Section 191], Rusty Pomaderris, is a shrub displaying masses of light creamy yellow flowers contrasting with mid green leaves.
Across the road from the Sydney Region Flora is Eriostemon myoporoides [Section 112], a small dainty with five white petals.

intro: The Mallee Shrublands [Section 211] is a mass of flower. Mallees (multi-trunked eucalypts) occur over much of dry central Australia. Dodonaea viscosa subsp. cuneata has showy green fruits all over it. Near the entrance to the Mallee is Acacia havilandiorum [Section 211], Needle Wattle, referring to
p: Dodonaea viscosa subsp. cuneata has showy green fruits all over it.
Near the entrance to the Mallee is Acacia havilandiorum [Section 211], Needle Wattle, referring to the tough foliage, with a multitude of golden flower balls along the stems.
Another Dodonaea or Hop Bush is Dodonaea lobulata [Section 211] which is exhibiting green-rusty pink fruits.
Westringia crassifolia [Section 211] an endangered species, has blue-mauve flowers.
Acacia montana [Section 211], the Mallee Wattle, has numerous bright yellow flowerheads appearing on sticky stalks.
Leptospermum coriaceum [Section 211], is a tea-tree with white flowers.
Phebalium squamulosum subsp. parvifolium [Section 211] is displaying its yellow flowers.
Lasiopetalum behrii [Section 211] is delightful with its beige flowers hanging down.
Leave the Mallee and walk along beside the Rainforest Gully, Zieria arborescens [Section 213] on the left hand side is showing its tiny white petalled flowers.
Further along to the right is Tasmania stipitata [Section 65], Pepper Bush, with its spiralling leaves and cream, slightly pink-tinged flowers growing out of the centre of the whorl.
On entering the Rainforest to your left is Acradenia euodiiformis [Section 64] a small tree of little cream flowers which are beginning to open.
Take the first path to the left and there is Hibbertia saligna [Section 15C] a small shrub with buttercup-yellow flowers.
To the right, Grevillea `Poorinda Royal Mantle' [Section 15D] is draping itself over the rocks exhibiting its cherry-red toothbrushes.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Higher up is Homoranthus darwinioides [Section 15E] which still has its pendulous yellow and maroon flowers contrasting against a grey-green foliage.

intro: The Gardens are so colourful with the spring array of flowers. Waratahs, in particular, reveal their red flower heads in many areas and Telopea speciosissima `Doug's Hybrid' at the main gates is no exception. Enjoy the plants in pots outside the Visitor Centre. Pimelea spectabilis is a small plant w
p: Waratahs, in particular, reveal their red flower heads in many areas and Telopea speciosissima `Doug's Hybrid' at the main gates is no exception.
Pimelea spectabilis is a small plant with large flower heads coloured white with a dash of pink.
Boronia `Tyalge Ruby' is laden with pink buds opening to dainty pink and white flowers.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
At the base of the stairs Telopea speciosissima `Wirrimbirra White' [Section 15D] is of medium size and bears many large white globular flower heads.
Grevillea `Poorinda Royal Mantle' [Section 15] is seen cascading down the rock face, with deep red toothbrush-like flowers mingling with the dark green foliage.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Tetratheca ciliata [Section 15S] is low and spreading and well covered with white, downturned flowers.
Phebalium whitei [Section 15S] bears golden yellow flowers on a small, erect shrub and nearby Pimelea ferruginea `Bonnie Petite' [Section 15S] has deep pink flowers borne in terminal heads.
Phebalium whitei [Section 15S] bears golden yellow flowers on a small, erect shrub and nearby Pimelea ferruginea `Bonnie Petite' [Section 15S] has deep pink flowers borne in terminal heads.
Not so brilliant, but most attractive, is Leptospermum `Pink Cascade' [Section 15S] which is a low, spreading Tea-tree crowned with delicate pink open flowers.

intro: Canberra City is a blaze with the lovely autumn colours of exotic trees. The Botanic Gardens, however, has only native trees and very few of those lose their leaves in winter.
p: Hypocalymma longifolium, in a pot close to the Visitors Centre doors, is a dwarf shrub with fluffy cerise-shaded flowers crowded along its small branches.
Crowea saligna [Section 174] could not be missed for this small shrub with waxy leaves is covered with bright pink starry flowers.
Banksia spinulosa [Section 126], one of many banksia species now flowering, has upright, cylindrical, gold flower spikes ribbed with red styles.

Correa reflexa `Maroondah Tricolour' [Section 119] bears fewer tubular flowers of red, cream and green.

In the Rock Garden, Epacris impressa [Section 15Q], Victoria's floral emblem, is really eye-catching for the upright branches are crowded with deep pink tubular flowers.
Find, also, Eucalyptus lansdowniana subsp. lansdowniana [Section 15R] bearing dense clusters of scarlet flowers on a small tree.

However Acacia saliciformis [Section 2], tall and pendulous, bears fluffy cream flower balls and Acacia fauntleroyi [Section 3] with a tall, bare trunk coated with reddish, peeling bark, is topped with branches covered with bright yellow flower balls.

Callistemon formosus [Section 11] is a small, dense tree decorated with lemon bottlebrushes.

p: At the bottom of the carpark there is a stand of NSW Christmas Bush, Ceratopetalum gummiferum [Section 142], all clad with their attractive pink calyces.
From a retaining wall the yellow kangaroo paw, Anigozanthos flavidus ‘Bush Dawn’ [Section 168], and the red-flowered form, Anigozanthos flavidus ‘Bush Sunset’ [Section 168], grow.
From a retaining wall the yellow kangaroo paw, Anigozanthos flavidus ‘Bush Dawn’ [Section 168], and the red-flowered form, Anigozanthos flavidus ‘Bush Sunset’ [Section 168], grow.
At the upper level the Smooth Barked Apple, Angophora costata subsp. costata [Section 168], with orange trunk and glossy green foliage bears clusters of white, feathery flowers.
See also the Swamp Foxtail, Pennisetum alopecuroides [Section 168], an attractive grass with many feathery purplish flower heads on upright stems.
Among the colourful plants in the pots outside the Visitor Centre, see the pink flowers of Scaevola ‘Pink Perfection’ creeping over the side of the pot.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)

Along Banks Walk, the backdrop to the bust of botanist Sir Joseph Banks is Banksia serrata [Section 174] which displays large, upright, cylindrical silky grey-green flower spikes amid the dark green foliage.
Walking up on the far side of the Rainforest Gully, Grevillea ‘Poorinda Royal Mantle’ [Section 124] is a dense ground cover endowed with many red toothbrush-like flowers.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Nearby, Callistemon ‘Howies Fire Glow’ [Section 124] bears red bottlebrush flowers, dusted with yellow, on an open shrub.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
It is worthwhile to venture down the stairs into the Rainforest Gully to view a flax-like plant, Helmholtzia glaberrima [Section 144] resplendent with soft pink plumes on long stems.
From here, look upwards to see the large, red flowers of the Dorrigo Waratah, Alloxylon pinnatum [Section 148].
Rubus fraxinifolius [Section 104], edging the Rainforest Gully, has prominent, mouth-watering red berries on a medium size shrub.
Further up, see Solanum campanulatum [Section 123], a low, scrambling plant with stems and leaf surfaces all covered with spines and bearing attractive mauve flowers.
Nearby is Crowea ‘Festival’ [Section 123], a small, neat rounded shrub with pink star-like flowers.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Around the corner Alyogyne huegelii [Section 123] dots the slope, displaying its hibiscus-like lilac flowers.
Continue upwards to see Acacia longissima [Section 123], a medium shrub with long, fine leaves and rod-like cream, fluffy flowers.
Beside the stairs above the shelter, Banksia lemanniana [Section 37] arranges its green flower spikes in a pendant fashion whereas most banksias have upright flower spikes.

From the lawns, the Coachwood Tree, Ceratopetalum apetalum [Section 37] is quite tall with calyces changing from cream to red, similar to the closely-related Christmas Bush, Ceratopetalum gummiferum [Section 37], beside it.

intro: This is a walk around the Rock Garden, where many small treasures are in flower. In front of the waterfall Lythrum salicaria [Section 15Q] displays its pink flowers on tall, erect stems. This plant is a perennial and enjoys wet feet. Beside the stairs Bulbine vagans [Section 15C] has succulent, stra
p: In front of the waterfall Lythrum salicaria [Section 15Q] displays its pink flowers on tall, erect stems.
Beside the stairs Bulbine vagans [Section 15C] has succulent, strappy leaves and is bright with star-like yellow flowers.
Baeckea virgata ‘Howies Sweet Midget’ [Section 15C] is a neat, rounded shrub covered with clusters of tiny white flowers and also coloured with new, red leaf tips.
Flowing down the rock face to the pools, Grevillea ‘Poorinda Royal Mantle’ [Section 15D] bears many red toothbrush-like flowers.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Beside the path the dazzling, orange clusters of small daisies in a tangle of soft, green foliage belong to Chrysocephalum apiculatum [Section 15D].
Garland Lily, Calostemma purpureum [Section 15B,15F] is a bulbous plant with heads of yellow-centered, pinkish, tubular flowers on top of bare, upright stems.
Crowded between rocks, Dampiera stricta [Section 15F] has soft mauve-blue flowers on upright stems.
The brilliant yellow and white straw daisies, Bracteantha varieties [Sections 15A, 15B, 15C], are self-seeded, adding extra colour to this area.
Also seen throughout this area are pockets of mounded plants with soft foliage dotted with small, mauve daisies which are Brachyscome spp.
At the top of the stairs, Persoonia linearis x pinifolia [Section 15H] is a large, pendulous shrub bearing yellow, cylindrical flower clusters amid soft, pine-like foliage.
Grevillea ‘Masons Hybrid’ [Section 15H] is another large shrub bearing pendent sprays of soft pinkish cream flowers.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Grevillea lanigera [Section 15W] is a prostrate plant with small, furry leaves brightened with cream and red flower clusters.
Looking upwards, kangaroo paws, Anigozanthos hybrids [Section 15H] look grand with copper-coloured flowers on long stems.
Lower down, Arthropodium milleflorum [Section 15H] daintily displays its tiny mauve flowers on long, arching stems.
Scaevola albida var. albida [Section 15H] is low and spreading and covered with vivid white fan flowers.
Nestled between rocks, Hibbertia vestata [Section 15L] sparkles with bright yellow flowers amid its ground-hugging foliage.
In this area other tiny plants include Scaevola sp. [Section 15R], with purple fan flowers, and Velleia trinervis [Section 15R] with rosettes of leaves and radiating stems of tiny lemon flowers.
[Section 15R], with purple fan flowers, and Velleia trinervis [Section 15R] with rosettes of leaves and radiating stems of tiny lemon flowers.
Goodenia amplexans [Section 15R], related to Velleia, has small yellow flowers along upright stems.
Not so small, Prostanthera aspalathoides [Section 15R] presents bright red, tubular flowers on an upright shrub.
Callistemon sp. [Section 4] is slender and graceful with an array of red bottlebrush flowers ...

intro: The attractive green tussocky grasses, Pennisetum alopecuroides [Section 168], in the car park continue to show off their decorative purplish feathery flower heads, although some are beginning to fade. Below the car park the stand of NSW Christmas Bush, Ceratopetalum gummiferum [Section 142], is so
p: The attractive green tussocky grasses, Pennisetum alopecuroides [Section 168], in the car park continue to show off their decorative purplish feathery flower heads, although some are beginning to fade.
Below the car park the stand of NSW Christmas Bush, Ceratopetalum gummiferum [Section 142], is so lovely with its covering of red calyces.
Banksia ‘Birthday Candles’, seen in the pot at the doors of the Visitor Centre, is dense and massed with small, erect green flower spikes just beginning to explode into handsome golden candles.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Brachyscome ‘Misty Mauve’ [Section 221], edging the path, is small and compact bearing small daisy flowers in varying shades of mauve.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Across the path Lomandra longifolia [Section 224] is another tussock-forming plant with long strappy leaves and odd-looking spiny yellow flowers on long stems.
In this bed Persoonia pinifolia [Section 224] is a graceful, small tree draped with cylindrical clusters of yellow flowers on the ends of the pendulous branches.
The burgundy-coloured ‘paws’ of Anigozanthos ‘Bush Ruby’ [Section 174] blend well with the rust and red coloured ‘paws’ of Anigozanthos ‘Bush Glow’ [Section 174].
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
The burgundy-coloured ‘paws’ of Anigozanthos ‘Bush Ruby’ [Section 174] blend well with the rust and red coloured ‘paws’ of Anigozanthos ‘Bush Glow’ [Section 174].
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)

On the higher side of the path Eremophila glabra ‘Murchison Magic’ [Section 210] has soft grey foliage dotted with red tubular flowers and on the lower side Crowea saligna [Section 174] bears cheery pink star-like flowers on a neat, small shrub.

On the higher side of the path Eremophila glabra ‘Murchison Magic’ [Section 210] has soft grey foliage dotted with red tubular flowers and on the lower side Crowea saligna [Section 174] bears cheery pink star-like flowers on a neat, small shrub.
In front of the Cafe building, Chrysocephalum semiamlexicaula [Section 131] is a low, straggly plant brilliant with small, glowing orange flower heads.
At the end of the building Callistemon viminalis [Section 143] is tall with dark, grooved trunks and deep red bottlebrush flowers dangling from arching branches.
Entering the Rock Garden, Bulbine vagans [Section 15C] is a bulbous plant with succulent narrow leaves bright with star-like yellow flowers.
Calostemma purpureum [Section 15B,15F] is another bulbous plant, commonly named Garland Lily, now bearing heads of yellow-centered pinkish tubular flowers.
Crinum flaccidum [Section 15B], the Murray or Darling Lily, is yet another bulbous plant with large, spectacular white trumpet-like flowers on top of long, upright stems.
Returning through the Rain Forest Gully, view the flax-like plant, Helmholtzia glaberrima [Section 144,145] with long, arching leaves and attractive pale pink flower plumes on deep red stems.

intro: This walk follows the Main Path, as described in the brochure ‘A walk along the new Main Path’. It starts at the far end of the Cafe building. Callistemon chisholmii [Section 11] is a graceful, open shrub with delicate, mixed pink and cream bottlebrush flowers suspended from its branches. Nearby Cal
p: Callistemon chisholmii [Section 11] is a graceful, open shrub with delicate, mixed pink and cream bottlebrush flowers suspended from its branches.
Nearby Callistemon pachyphyllus [Section 11] is an older straggly shrub bearing larger red bottlebrushes.
Admire the small patch of daisies which includes the yellow straw daisy Bracteantha bracteata [Section 8] and, further on, the soft mauve daisy flowers of Olearia rudis [Section 8].
Admire the small patch of daisies which includes the yellow straw daisy Bracteantha bracteata [Section 8] and, further on, the soft mauve daisy flowers of Olearia rudis [Section 8].
Then a bed of colour displaying a selection of Brachyscome varieties [Section 8] with small daisies shaded mauve mixed with shades of yellow.

At the corner Grevillea rivularis [Section 191], with sharp, divided leaves, extends its long branches with pink toothbrush-like flowers above the long-flowering Crowea exalata [Section 191] which bears small, pink star-like flowers.

At the corner Grevillea rivularis [Section 191], with sharp, divided leaves, extends its long branches with pink toothbrush-like flowers above the long-flowering Crowea exalata [Section 191] which bears small, pink star-like flowers.
Along this winding path, Goodenia heterophylla subsp. montana [Section 191] has prostrate stems bearing small yellow flowers.
Scaevola ramosissima [Section 191], also with trailing stems, has large, purple fan flowers.
Spyridium sp. [Section 191] is an upright, small shrub bearing clusters of tiny white flowers encircled by greyish floral leaves.
The Fringed Lily, Thysanotus juncifolius [Section 191], has deep purple flowers with three fringed petals on long stems which hug the ground.
To the left of the seat, in the wall, is the fossil of the seed-fern, Glossopteris, behind which are the yellow flower spikes of Banksia spinulosa var. spinulosa [Section 191].
At the top end of this area a small display garden contains Crowea saligna [Section 191] with fresh, green foliage and bright pink flowers on a small shrub, Goodenia sp.

At the top end of this area a small display garden contains Crowea saligna [Section 191] with fresh, green foliage and bright pink flowers on a small shrub, Goodenia sp. with small yellow flowers on trailing stems and the lovely white Flannel Flowers, Actinotu
with small yellow flowers on trailing stems and the lovely white Flannel Flowers, Actinotus helianthi [Section 191] which have been flowering for many months.
The path winds through the Eucalypt Lawn to the Rock Garden where the orange glow of the flowers of Chrysocephalum apiculatum [Section 4], edging the path, is quite dazzling.
Banksia aemula [Section 16] is a dense shrub laden with pale green cylindrical flower spikes.
At the bottom of the rock cutting Eremophila glabra ‘Murchison Magic’ [Section 210], illuminated with salmon-coloured, tubular flowers amid the grey-green foliage, is quite a picture.

The vista along the Sydney Region gully overlooks large tree ferns, Dicksonia antarctica [Section 191] and the long sword-like leaves of the Gymea Lily, Doryanthes excelsa [Section 191] ...

Plants seen along the path on the far side of this gully include the Native Fuchsia, Epacris longiflora [Section 191], a rather straggly plant with eye-catching red tubular flowers tipped with white and a tall, willowy wattle, Acacia saliciformis [Section 191]

Baeckea linifolia [Section 191], in the gully, is a dainty small shrub with arching branches laden with tiny white flowers.
The vivid gold flower spikes, seen across the gully, are those of Banksia spinulosa var. spinulosa [Section 191].
Crossing the road, Acacia o’shanesii [Section 191] is another small tree with pendulous branches.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
The NSW Christmas Bush, Ceratopetalum gummiferum [Section 191], seen along this path continues to be clad with its waxy red calyces which resemble flowers.

Leptospermum rupestre [Section 191, a teatree, is a small shrub with spreading branches covered with white petalled flowers. Returning on the other side of the gully, see the small bed still displaying Flannel Flowers, Actinotus helianthi [Section 191], with s

Returning on the other side of the gully, see the small bed still displaying Flannel Flowers, Actinotus helianthi [Section 191], with soft, grey-green velvety foliage and attractive white furry flowers.
Crowea saligna [Section 191] with waxy pink flowers amid the waxy green leaves is also in this garden, as well as Goodenia sp.

Crowea saligna [Section 191] with waxy pink flowers amid the waxy green leaves is also in this garden, as well as Goodenia sp. [Section 191] a ground hugging plant with trailing branches studded with bright yellow flowers.
Across the path, Platysace clelandii [Section 191] is a small, rounded shrub clustered with minute white flowers.

Scaevola albida [Section 124] is a suckering ground cover dotted with small mauve fan flowers.
Around the corner, Grevillea ‘Robyn Gordon’ [Section 124] displays its lovely terminal red sprays of flowers on a low, open shrub.

Correa alba var. alba [Section 107], with silver edged leaves and white star flowers, hugs the base of the magnificent old Eucalyptus mannifera [Section 107] with mottled grey trunk.
Plectranthus argentatus [Section 110] is a suckering, herbaceous plant with large, felt-like grey-green leaves and tiny mauve, almost white, flowers along upright stems.
Further back is Callistemon ‘Glasshouse Country’ [Section 110] displaying its lovely pink bottlebrush flowers on a neat shrub of medium size.

Overlooking it is Dampiera stricta [15F], a suckering plant with soft blue flowers.
Lomandra leucocephala subsp. robusta [Section 15W] has clusters of tiny cream flowers tightly packed around the stems at regular intervals.
Ascending the stairs, the masses of blue-tinted, almost white, daisy flowers with dark centres are those of Olearia ramulosa [Section 15A].
Grevillea ‘Masons Hybrid’ [Section 15H] is large and dense and bears many large, terminal clusters of flowers with red and cream tonings.

Above the Rock Garden is a planting of Crowea ‘Festival’ [Section 123].

Solanum campanulatum [Section 123] has soft mauve flowers with ground running stems and leaves covered with fine prickles ....

A bed of daisies includes the compact Bracteantha bracteata 'Diamond Head' [Section 8] with small yellow flowers dotted over the low growing plant.

p: Starting near the base of the waterfall, the bulbous plant Bulbine vagans [Section 15C] bears bright star-like yellow flowers amid the succulent, narrow leaves.

Two very small plants worth viewing are Boronia nana var. hyssopifolia [Section 15L], with tiny cream flowers which change to red on ageing borne on stems trailing over the bank, and the ACT floral emblem, Wahlenbergia gloriosa [Section 15L], with large blue f

intro: Canberra's golden autumn shades are bright and picturesque. Likewise the fascinating banksias so come and enjoy this banksia walk where the most colourful plants are identified. More information can be found in the Banksia pamphlet available from the Visitor Centre. Compare the leaf shapes and sizes
p: On Banks Walk, the backdrop to the bust of Sir Joseph Banks is Banksia serrata [Section 174] which flowered earlier this year.
Outside the Visitor Centre doors Banksia 'Birthday Candles' flows over the side of a pot and is massed with small cylindrical pale gold flower spikes about 4 cm tall.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
In front of the Banks Building Banksia 'Giant Candles' [Section143] glows with golden flower spikes 30 cm tall.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
In the same garden, Banksia 'Austraflora Pigmy Possum' [Section 143] is a dwarf, spreading plant with well concealed greyish flower spikes seen below the branches.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Closer to the building Marsh Banksia, Banksia paludosa [Section 143], displays its almost coppery, finer flower spikes.
Note also the low growing Correa 'Dusky Bells' [Section 143] bearing dusky pink tubular flowers.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Banksia ericifolia var. ericifolia [Section 143], Heath Banksia, is an ageing rounded shrub with many spent grey flower spikes, many with retained fruits.
Admire Callistemon citrinus 'Austraflora Firebrand' [Section 32] a medium size shrub which lovingly displays its cherry-red bottlebrush flowers.
Swamp Banksia, Banksia robur [Section28], still has juvenile bottle green flower spikes which, on maturing, change to lemon and so to a chocolate colour.

Banksia spinulosa var. collina [Section 28], Hill Banksia, is large and rounded and dotted with pencil-fine green immature flower spikes already changing to dull gold, but not yet to its most colourful golden candlesticks.
Banksia conferta var. penicillata [Section 28], further off the road, is a large, rounded shrub, with an abundance of spent flower spikes, also bearing many small yellow flower spikes.
From the far end of this section, find Banksia integrifolia var. compar [Section 28], a small, dense tree with white backed leaves.

Up the road, Banksia aemula [Section 191] is dense with almost round woolly yellow-green flower spikes.

intro: This lovely autumn weather makes pleasurable walking where flowers, including wattles, banksias and others are so colourful. p: To start, view Acacia aphylla [Section 221] in a pot outside the Visitor Centre door.
The walk commences up above the Nursery to find Acacia jibberdingensis from a small WA town called Jibberding.
At the cross roads, Thryptomene saxicola ‘Pink Lace’ [Section 41] is a small, open shrub covered with small, pink flowers so desirable for floral arrangement.
Taking the marked road, Pittosporum rhombifolium [Section 96] is a slim, small tree with branches heavy with bunches of orange fruits and with glossy green leaves.
This area contains many correas including Correa ‘Dusky Bells’ [Section 106], a low, spreading shrub, always with red tubular flowers dangling amid the dense foliage.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Correa backhousiana [Section 106] is also a dense shrub of medium size bearing larger tubular, cream flowers.

Taking the narrow, mossy green path, Hakea suaveolens [Section 75] is about 35 years old with a wandering old trunk leading eventually to branches of long needle foliage and ovoid masses of perfumed cream flowers tipped with pink styles.
Almost opposite is a group of Crowea exalata plants [Section 150] massed with brilliant pink starry flowers.
In this section of wattles, Acacia saliciformis [Section 77] is a graceful tree with pendulous branches clad with clusters of cream, woolly flower balls.
Acacia iteaphylla [Section 77], Port Lincoln Wattle, is a dense, many-trunked shrub yellow with soft flower balls.
who could not admire it! Behind is the Sunshine Wattle, Acacia terminalis [Section 77] with fishbone-like leaves and smothered with pale, fluffy, flower balls.

Banksia oblongifolia [Section 75] is a low, spreading shrub displaying many green juvenile spikes maturing to interesting grey-green flower spikes.

The border plant Chrysocephalum apiculatum [Section 4] is so colourful with its small clusters of orange flowers.

Chloanthes stoechadis [Section 44] has narrow wrinkled leaves which almost conceal its interesting grey-green tubular flowers.

p: This walk is along the Main Path starting from the far end of the Cafe building where many banksias are flourishing, including Banksia spinulosa var. collina [Section 131] clad with attractive gold flower spikes.
Opposite, a very small Acacia alata [Section 240] bears fluffy golden flower balls along its unusual ‘winged’ stems (the wings are actually flattened phyllodes).
Emu Bush, Eremophila maculata [Section 9], is a small, neat shrub bright with yellow trumpet-shaped flowers.
Rounding the corner, there is a patch of bright yellow straw daisies, Bracteantha bracteata [Section 8].
Correa ‘Dusky Bells’ [Section 30] is low and spreading, with red tubular flowers dangling amid the foliage.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Grevillea rosmarinifolia sens. lat. [Section 30] is also a low, spreading shrub dotted with yellow buds and flowers.
Banksia integrifolia var. integrifolia [Section 30] is tall and elegant with silver-backed leaves and small, lemon flower spikes.

Grevillea paniculata [Section 26] is quite open and tipped with green buds and perfumed cream flowers.
Grevillea sp. aff. miqueliana (Nullica) [Section 26] is a small, rounded shrub decorated with soft pink-red pendent spider flowers.

spinulosa [Section 25] and the deep gold of the flower spikes of Banksia ericifolia var. ericifolia.

The small garden in front of the waterfall is brightened with the small orange flowers of Lechenaultia formosa [Section 15D].
Banksia aemula [Section 16] has an abundance of squat pale yellow flower spikes.

Grevillea lanigera [Section 15W], brilliant with pink spider-like flowers, is quite dense and hugs the ground down this slope.

Nearby, Guichenotia macrantha [Section 15F] is so lovely, with pink, down-turned flowers.
In a small garden not far away, a miniature shrub, Epacris impressa (Mimosa Rocks National Park) [Section 15N], is a picture for it is well clad with coral pink tubular flowers.
Ground cover Grevillea maxwellii [Section 15P] has sharp, divided leaves which almost conceal the interesting deep red grape-like buds and flowers.

Dampiera sericantha [Section 15R] is a neater, dwarf herb with flowers a lighter shade of blue.
Lasiopetalum involucratum [Section 15R] is a dense, small shrub with cheery, pink flowers amid many buds covered with rust-coloured calyces.
Correa pulchella ‘Mist Pink’ [Section 15S] is picturesque with pendent pink tubular flowers.

Grevillea victoriae [Section 37] too, is a picture with rust coloured, grape-like flowers pendent in a neat shrub.

p: below the windows of the Visitor Centre, Hakea crassinervia [Section 221] is a low, almost prostrate, spreading shrub with branches well crowded with cheery red flower balls which have a covering of cream styles resembling a pin cushion.
Nearby Eucalyptus caesia subsp. magna [Section 221], with long arching silver-grey branches, displays its large pendent frilly pink flowers and buds.
Across the path, Grevillea diminuta [Section 222] is a low, dense shrub thickly covered with pendent rust-red flower clusters.
Along the colourful Banks Walk, Templetonia retusa [Section 174] has large red pea- shaped flowers along the many upright branches.

At the far end of the Hudsons’ Cafe building, Banksia spinulosa var. collina [Section 131] bears mustard-coloured cylindrical, upright flower spikes and Banksia ‘Giant Candles’ [Section 143] is alight with elongated gold flower spikes.
collina [Section 131] bears mustard-coloured cylindrical, upright flower spikes and Banksia ‘Giant Candles’ [Section 143] is alight with elongated gold flower spikes.

Note nearby, Grevillea dielsiana [Section 28], a rather misshapen shrub with finely divided leaves, has attractive yellow flower clusters, tipped red.

Around the corner and into the Sydney Region flora plantings, where Crowea saligna [Section 191] displays large, pink, star-like flowers over a small, neat shrub.
Compare this species with Crowea exalata [Section 191] with finer foliage and smaller pink flowers.
Thryptomene saxicola ‘Pink Lace’ [Section 19] is a dainty small shrub bearing tiny pink flowers along the upright branches.
Opposite, Hakea invaginata [Section 22] is of medium size, clad with clusters of cream globular flowers.

p: Go down the stairs to the car park and on your right is Hakea crassinervia [Section 221], with red blooms, some of which are still coming out.
Next to it is the dainty Westringia crassifolia [Section 221] with tiny pale blue flowers and lots of buds which have yet to open.
Allocasuarina thalassoscopica [Section 174] has small, reddish flowers, not as showy as Hakea crassinervia but well worth seeing.
Walk past the bus shelter and here are two forms of Chrysocephalum apiculatum [Section 174], the green-leaf form and the grey-leaf form.
Near the bridge is Odixia angusta [Section 66a], a small shrub with a few prominent white daisy flowers.

There is a large patch of Grevillea linearifolia [Section 26] which stretches between two paths.
Close by is Grevillea flexuosa [Section 26] with grey-green leaves and dense cream flower clusters like candles at the ends of its branches.
Grevillea juniperina [Section 24] is different again from these two species as it is a rounded shrub with clusters of dark red flowers.

Westringia glabra [Section 6] has light green foliage with clusters of mauve flowers and the whole plant smells vaguely of mint.
In the garden bed opposite is Bauera rubioides [Section 7], a compact shrub about a metre in height and the same wide, with dainty pink flowers.
Grevillea aspleniifolia [Section 120] is a huge plant with mauve toothbrush-type flowers and will be flowering for a considerable time to come.
Then on to Acacia podalyriifolia [Section 126] with its silver-grey foliage and bright golden flower balls.

intro: This is a spring walk along the Main Path which features only a few of the many lovely flowers on view at present. p: Ascending the ramp in front of the Visitor Centre, the Snowy River Wattle, Acacia boormanii [Section 212], glows yellow with soft, fluffy flower balls making a bright backdrop.
At the top of the ramp Westringia glabra [Section 212] is quite small and bears bright purple bugle-shaped flowers.
Walking through the Rainforest Gully with its many shades of green, Zieria arborescens [Section 148] is quite a large shrub clad with dark green foliage and dotted with sprays of tiny white flowers.
Nearby a sassafras, Doryphora sassafras [Section 65], is a neat small tree with dark serrated leaves and prominent white flowers.
The Rock Garden abounds with flowers and along this path Choryzema cordatum x Choryzema varium [Section 4] is a small, spreading plant bearing red pea flowers.
Dampiera sp. [Section 15R] is a low, suckering herb bearing lovely deep blue flowers.
The straggly, woody Hakea purpurea [Section 20] is charmed with flame red flowers amid its sharp needles.
See the graceful Acacia cognata [Section 19] with willowy branches clad with soft fine foliage mingling with soft, fluffy yellow flower balls.
Edging this bed Eutaxia obovata [Section 19] has low, spreading branches covered with perfectly arranged leaves and yellow pea flowers with a reddish keel.
Grevillea aspleniifolia [Section 191] has an interesting habit with its long trunk and branches spreading low and horizontal with long, narrow leaves and pink toothbrush-like flowers.
Hardenbergia violacea [Section 191], covered with its deep purple pea flowers, boldly weaves over this shrub.
Indigofera australis [Section 191] is an open shrub with sprays of lilac pea flowers among the bluish-green foliage.
Hibbertia saligna [Section 191] bears bright yellow flowers among dull green leaves on a low, upright plant.
Towards the end of this curving path Grevillea baueri subsp. asperula [Section 191] is picturesque with a covering of red spider-like flowers.
Crossing the road, Eriostemon myoporoides subsp. acutus [Section 112] is a dense shrub bearing many white star flowers.

Pomaderris intermedia [Section 175] also has sprays of soft yellow flowers crowning small to medium size open shrubs.
Acacia cultriformis ‘Austraflora Cascade’ [Section 226], covered with yellow flower balls, drapes its pendulous branches over a retaining wall in the car park.
Closer to the Visitor Centre Acacia pycnantha [Section 224], Australia’s Floral Emblem, proudly displays its lovely golden flower balls over a small tree.
Quite an eye-catcher in the display outside the Visitor Centre is the small plant Lechenaultia formosa flaunting its red flowers over the side of a pot.

Along Banks Walk, bright with flowers, Grevillea ‘Scarlet Sprite’ [Section 174] bears scarlet spider-like flowers over a neat, fine leafed shrub and Prostanthera florifera [Section 174], still very small, bears deep purple bugle flowers.

Trace the perfume and flowers of the renowned Brown Boronia, Boronia megastigma ‘Virtuoso’[Section 15F].
Above the steps Acacia boormanii [Section 2], massed with fluffy yellow flower balls, is one of many wattles in this section.
Several neat, rounded shrubs covered with pale pink buds and many white starry flowers are Eriostemon myoporoides [Sections 122 and 123].
Close to the covered shelter, Grevillea lanigera [Section 37] is a dense ground cover dotted with deep red flowers.
Over the path is a waratah, Telopea speciosissima ‘Wirrimbirra White’ [Section 37], with large very pale green buds about to explode into large, almost white flowers.
Along the top path Hakea coriacea [Section 37] is tall and many branched, crowned with long thin leaves and lovely poker-shaped lolly-pink flower spikes, so picturesque as they sway in the breeze.
Hakea francisiana [Section 37] is there too, with similar shaped white flower clusters.

Quite close, on the same side, is Westringia longifolia [Section 119] with showy mauve flowers.
Acacia howitti [Section 110] is a dense, large shrub / small tree with pendulous branches arching over the small path.
Wandering back towards the Cafe, on your right is Indigofera australia [Section 114] with large sprays of purple pea-flowers.

Above the waterfall, Telopea mongaensis x speciosissima [Section 15D] is magnificently covered with red flower heads.
Gymea Lily, Doryanthes excelsa [Section 15C], displays its large cluster of red flowers atop an elongated spike which is surrounded by large sword-like leaves.

Edging the lawns, Patersonia umbrosa [Section 15R], a native iris, displays its large, three-petalled deep mauve flowers on upright stems.
Seek out Boronia heterophylla [Section 15R], which bears deep pink bell-shaped flowers so fragrantly perfumed.

p: Hibbertia stellaris [Section 174], beside Sir Joseph Banks sculpture, is small, round and bright with orange scalloped flowers.

Banksia oblongifolia [Section 191], along the crossroad is a low, spreading shrub well covered with lime-green flower spikes.

p: Eremophila glabra 'Murchison Magic' [Section 210] has a few of its small scarlet flowers showing, but its real atttraction is as a foliage contrast plant.
Just a few paces along can be seen the soft lipstick pink flowers of Crowea saligna [Section 174].

Following the Main Path past the kiosk you will come to the "Friends Lounge", where there are many Croweas in flower [Section 240] They are best seen from near the magnificent silvery trunks of a pair of Eucalyptus mannifera or Brittle Gums [Section 240].
On the far end of this garden bed is an excellent specimen of a Banksia integrifolia (prostrate form) [Section 240] which is just coming into flower.
Outside the Banks building is another interesting banksia, Banksia 'Giant Candles' [Section 143] which holds its flowers on tall cones, approximately 25 cm long.

p: Just past the entrance to the Ellis Rowan Building Crowea exalata [MP8-9, Section 13] is looking cheerful.
Nearby the cultivar Correa ‘Betts Red’ [MP8-9, Section 13] is displaying its red bells.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
At the end of the building three Banksia spinulosa varieties [MP11-12, Section 131] are flowering well.
Continue along the path to where Banksia ericifolia var. ericifolia [MP29, Section 30] is in flower.
Further on you will see Correa alba var. alba [MP31, Section 30] in flower.
At the end of the section look for Banksia integrifolia var. integrifolia [MP32, Section 30] and the prostrate form beside it.

intro: In this cold weather you would expect to see very few plants in flower, but this week’s walk takes you through parts of the Gardens which have a few floral surprises.
p: On your right is Grevillea diminuta [Section 222], with rusty red flowers in pendulous clusters.
On your left is Westringia crassifolia [Section 221], a spreading shrub with small purple flowers.
Continuing along the footpath with the car park on your right, you can see Callistemon subulatus [Section 221] with dark red flower spikes just beginning to emerge.
A little further on is Grevillea iaspicula [Section 221], or Wee Jasper Spider Flower, with clusters of beautiful dark pink and cream flowers.
On your left are several bushes of the spectacular Calothamnus quadrifidus [Section 12] with silvery green foliage and red flower spikes emerging at the base of the stems.
Turn right at the path just before the road junction, where you can find a large bush of Grevillea rosmarinifolia [Section 180] with clusters of tiny red flowers at the ends of the stems.

On your right, just past the picnic tables, are some spectacular banksias in flower, including the orange flower spikes of Banksia ericifolia var. ericifolia [Section 180], and the stately Banksia robur [Section 180] with large, leathery leaves and yellow-gree
ericifolia [Section 180], and the stately Banksia robur [Section 180] with large, leathery leaves and yellow-green flower heads.
In amongst the banksias is Callistemon citrinus[Section 180], with dark red flower spikes just emerging.

p: At the bottom of the waterfall Lechenaultia formosa [Section 15V] bears its bright yellow flowers over a very small plant.

no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)

Nearby, Hakea myrtoides [Section 15P] is also prostrate with trailing branches massed with crimson flowers.

Correa pulchella ‘Pink Mist’ [Section 15S] is a dense, rounded shrub with pink tubular flowers dangling from the branches.

no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
The low, compact Crowea exalata ‘Bindelong Compact’ [Section 15S] is a wee beauty decorated with deep red, changing to pink, star flowers.

Find Hakea crassinervia [Section 20], a long-flowering plant with long, arching branches bearing fascinating globular pincushion-like pink and white flowers.

Nearby Hakea bakeriana [Section 21] conceals its remarkable flowers on the mature stems and old woody branches inside the foliage.

Time now to stroll towards the Nursery to view a tea-tree, Leptospermum squarrosum [Section 44], an erect shrub which displays its clusters of bright pink ‘apple blossom’ flowers under the foliage.

intro: Throughout our fair city and in these gardens, wattles are beginning to show their lovely golden flowers, grevilleas are beginning to flower and banksias continue to flower. A mint bush, Prostanthera sp. [Section 210] is a small shrub dotted with purple bugle shaped flowers.
Grevillea ‘Poorinda Queen’ [Section 124] shows off its spider-like apricot flowers on a medium size, spreading shrub.

Banksia integrifolia var. aquilonia [Section 37] has orange flower spikes amid long narrow leaves.

Allocasuarina torulosa [Section 40], forest oak, is a tall tree, brilliant with copper coloured male spikes mixed with fine green foliage.

intro: Above the car park to the left of the Visitor Centre is a group of wattles, Acacia genistifolia [Section 225], all dotted with cream, fluffy flowers over these open shrubs. p: Above the car park to the left of the Visitor Centre is a group of wattles, Acacia genistifolia [Section 225], all dotted with cream, fluffy flowers over these open shrubs.
The Mallee Section has numerous flowering plants which include Pimelea sp. [Section 211] scattered about the garden.
Micromyrtus ciliata [Section 211] is another small, dainty shrub with lateral branches massed with deep pink buds just exploding into small white flowers.
Grevillea rosmarinifolia [Section 211] is a small, dense, fine leafed shrub which conceals its deep red spider flowers below the foliage.

Hybanthus floribundus subsp. adpressus [Section 211] has many short, upright stems clad with pale blue to cream flowers; the curved leaves are pressed upwards against the stems, hence the subspecies name.

Further along this narrow, winding path, past the patient, old Mallee Fowl standing on the large nest, waiting … to where Bossiaea walkeri [Section 211], Cactus Bossiaea, has long flattened, leafless grey stems which, being a plant of the dry inland, actually
Acacia boormanii [Section 2] has such soft foliage, now covered with yellow buds awaiting a few warm days, like so many wattles, to flower.
Acacia costiniana [Section 15K] in the Rock Garden, is a small shrub with leaves which seem to hug the branches which are brightened with yellow flower balls.
Acacia flexifolia [Section 3] is low, dense and pretty with small yellow, fluffy flower balls along the upright stems.
Across the road, Hakea purpurea [Section 20] displays its small, purplish red flowers close to the upright branches.

Tis worth a walk towards the Sydney Region Flora to view Hardenbergia violacea [Section 112], a ground-hugging creeper purple with pea flowers surrounding the mottled grey trunk of one of the many Eucalyptus mannifera [Section 112] trees.

Returning, one of the many banksias is Banksia occidentalis [Section 27], a tall open shrub with bare pink and grey mottled trunks and lovely cylindrical flower spikes coloured lemon with bright red styles.

intro: On leaving the Visitor Centre turn right and wander down towards the first path on the left, where Acacia cognata ‘Green Mist’ [Section 210] is sitting right on the corner. p: Here also, look up toward the top of the building where Acacia covenyi [Section 212], with its grey-green leaves and sprays of bright yellow balls, is almost in full flower.
Further on are several small shrubs of Grevillea rosmarinifolia [Section 182], with clusters of red and cream spider flowers at the end of the stems.
Further still is Acacia podalyriifolia [Section 126], with silver grey foliage and golden ball-shaped flowers assuring us spring is on the way.
A few steps away still is Banksia spinulosa [Section 126] with its yellow-orange spikes, some of which have just flowered while others have already changed to brown.
Almost at the end of this bed is a slight bush, Grevillea ‘Poorinda Diadem’ [Section 126], with large yellow-apricot coloured flowers, typically in clusters.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Wend your way to the triangular garden which has some small, slender but showy plants of Baeckea crassifolia [Section 17] covered in tiny, pale pink flowers.

In the same bed is Epacris calvertiana var. calvertiana [Section 17], covered with lots of small, delightful cream tubular flowers.

Further up the hill are quite a few shrubs of Crowea ‘Festival’ [Section 123] covered in bright, pink, star-shaped flowers, thriving in spite of the Armillaria Root Rot that has damaged the Acacias and Eucalypts growing here.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Next to it is Banksia oblongifolia [Section 37] covered in small spikes of green-yellow.
Then comes Banksia ericifolia var. ericifolia [Section 37] with larger cones in various shades of orange, depending on when they came into flower.

Then there is a grafted Western Australian species, Banksia media [Section 37], with its yellow cylindrical spikes.

p: A little way past the Café is Eriostemon difformis [Section 131], a small shrub with red buds some of which have burst out into dainty white flowers.

Grevillea paniculata [Section 26] is covered in creamy-white coloured clusters of flowers making the plant very easily seen.

In the area of grevilleas, Grevillea wilsonii [Section 27,26] is a low shrub with fine, sharp divided leaves and showy erect scarlet flowers, mostly in clusters.
Grevillea johnsonii x wilsonii [Section 24] is tall with long segmented leaves and lovely waxy red flowers.
Kennedia macrophylla [Section 112] is a twining mass of soft green vine, decorated with large burnt red pea flowers.
Seen along the path curving through the Sydney Region Gully, Jacksonia scoparia [Section 191] is vivid with an abundance of bright yellow pea flowers on an upright shrub.
Flannel Flowers, Actinotus helianthi ‘Federation Star’ [Section 191], with large white velvet-like flowers amid velvety green-grey foliage, grow here and there.
Cassinia denticulata [Section 191] is laden with flower heads, dense with minute cream flowers.
Scaevola ramosissima var. ramosissima [Section 191] is a ground hugging plant with stems bearing large mauve fan-flowers.
Hibbertia diffusa [Section 191] is also ground hugging, dense with bright yellow flowers.
Boronia microphylla [Section 191] continues to be densely covered with pink buds maturing to paler small flowers.
On your way back, wander through the restful Eucalypt Lawn to the Rock Garden, passing by Hakea trineura [Section 20] laden with long pendent yellow and burnt red flowers ...
In front of the waterfall see the Royal Bluebell, Canberra’s Floral Emblem, Wahlenbergia gloriosa [Section 15V].
Read about the treasured Wollemi Pine, Wollemia nobilis [Section 110], inside the large cage.
Relax in the coolness of the Rainforest where a tree, Callicoma serratifolia [Section 146] bears many fluffy, globular flower heads.

intro: Tis summer … tis warm … flowers continue to be plentiful. So, to start, view those in the Tasmanian Garden. There seem to be many white flowers which include numerous Ozothamnus species. Ozothamnus expansifolius [Section 231] is a short shrub with terminal heads of tiny cream flowers. Ozothamnus eri
p: Ozothamnus expansifolius [Section 231] is a short shrub with terminal heads of tiny cream flowers.
Ozothamnus ericifolius [Section 231,232] is a taller shrub with similar dense clusters of larger daisies.
Pentachondra involucrata [Section 230] is a dwarf, dense plant covered with upright spikes of small white tubular flowers with mouth of fine frilly star petals.

Senecio linearifolius [Section 236], with terminal sprays of yellow daisies, lines the bank of the northern pool.
Above, Pelargonium australe [Section 142] has sprays of flowers which are mauve, almost white, with purple veins all over low shrubs with soft ripply leaves.
Near the seat Dianella tasmanica [Section 142] is a strappy, spreading flax-like plant with bright blue flowers that have bright yellow anthers.
Behind the seat, a leatherwood cultivar, Eucryphia lucida ‘Ballerina’ [Section 142], is a neat small tree decorated with open-petalled pink flowers.
Along the far side of the Rainforest Gully, Native Elderberry, Cuttsia viburnea [Section 125] is a large rounded shrub, dense with shining toothed leaves and large sprays of white perfumed flowers.
Kangaroo paw, Anigozanthos flavidus [Section 126], displays its red and green ‘paw’ flowers on long, upright bare stems.
Opposite Callistemon ‘Harkness’ [Section 124] is tall with dark, grooved trunks and weeping habit displaying bright red bottlebrush flowers.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)

Melaleuca ambigua x capitata [Section 119] is decorated with soft pink fluffy flower balls while opposite, Jacksonia scoparia [Section 119], with bare trunk, has a canopy of long fine leaves and sprays of yellow pea-flowers.

Melaleuca ambigua x capitata [Section 119] is decorated with soft pink fluffy flower balls while opposite, Jacksonia scoparia [Section 119], with bare trunk, has a canopy of long fine leaves and sprays of yellow pea-flowers.
In the distance, with a foreground of grasses, the clusters of red flowers on extended bare stems of the Gymea Lily, Doryanthes excelsa [Section 8] can be seen.
Arriving at the Rock Garden, which contains a huge variety of flowers, see Leptospermum ‘Aphrodite’ [Section 15C].
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Marvel at and read about the rare Wollemi Pine, Wollemia nobilis [Section 110], safe in a decorative cage.

Further uphill, in the triangular bed, Hibbertia stellaris [Section 17] is a dwarf, dense shrub alight with orange flowers and Ptilotus nobilis [Section 17] has upright stems with rather large green-cream fluffy conical flowers.
