Philotheca myoporoides [Section 240] has masses of white flowers with pink buds.
Isopogon anethifolius [Section 240] has vigorous upright linear foliage with bright yellow ‘drumstick’ flowers.
Commersonia (Rulingia) magniflora [Section 240] on your left, has strongly scented white flowers with pink centres.

Go left up the stairs towards the Main Path and continue up the hill to see on your left Melaleuca fulgens ‘Hot Pink’ [Section 10], with attractive bottlebrush flowers that are hot pink with gold stamens.
On your left are several Bulbine glauca [Section 8], with spires of lemon flowers opening sequentially.
Look up to your left to see one of the most spectacular flowers in the Gardens Doryanthes excelsa [Section 8], or Gymea Lily, just beginning to open.
Telopea speciosissima [Section 30] also on your left forms another spectacular display.
On your left is Kunzea parvifolia [Section 30], a large bush with fluffy white flowers scented strongly with honey and much beloved by insects.

intro: There are so many plants in flower at this time that it is hard to choose which ones to feature.
p: As you leave the Visitor Information Centre look to your left to see Dendrobium × delicatum [Section 212], an orchid with clusters of white flowers and oblong green foliage.
On your right in a pot is Gastrolobium involutum [Section 221], with bright orange/yellow pea flowers on graceful fine linear foliage.
Further on your right in a pot is Swainsona formosa [Section 221], or Sturt’s Desert Pea, with pale green leaves and bright red pea flowers.
Notice in a pot on your right Hibbertia stellaris [Section 174], or Orange Stars, with masses of orange star flowers on wiry foliage.
In a small bed on your right before crossing the bridge are clumps of Conostylis candicans subsp. candicans [Section 174], with yellow flower-heads on fine grey strappy foliage.
Look high on your left to see Vesselowskya rubifolia [Section 210], a large shrub with serrated green leaves and fluffy racemes of pink and cream flowers.
As you cross the bridge notice on your right Olearia argophylla [Section 66], a tall shrubby daisy with many white flower-heads with gold centres.
Pimelea ferruginea ‘Magenta Mist’ [Section 131], on your left in the Ellis Rowan Garden, has bright pink flower-heads on neat foliage.
On your right towards the top of the hill is Homoranthus flavescens [Section 9] with acid yellow blooms layered on a small bush.
Melaleuca diosmifolia [Section 9], on your right, has green brush-like flowers on neat darker green foliage.
Doryanthes excelsa [Section 8], or Gymea Lily, is found only in coastal areas near Sydney, New South Wales.
Telopea ‘Canberry Gem’ [Section 30], also on your left, forms another spectacular display.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Close by on your left is another waratah Telopea mongaensis [Section 30], a smaller bush with deeper red flowers, commonly known as the Monga Waratah or Braidwood Waratah.
Turn back now and veer right to see Pultenaea villosa [Section 30] on your right.

Also on your right is Bauera rubioides [Section 8], or Dog Rose, a large bush with bright pink flowers en masse.The species is widespread throughout coastal and in moist mountain areas in New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania.

intro: We will walk to the Rock Garden today, as there are many choice plants in flower there.
p: On your left as you turn right is Doryanthes palmeri [Section 114] or Giant Spear Lily.
Enter the Rock Garden up the steps to see on your right Doryanthes excelsa, or Gymea Lily [Section 15d].
Also on your right in a pot is Hibbertia pedunculata [Section 15d], with bright yellow flowers on fine creeping foliage.
Further on your right is Grevillea ‘Poorinda Royal Mantle’ [Section 15d], with red toothbrush flowers on a vigorous sprawling groundcover.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
As you continue up the hill on your left is Leptospermum variabile [Section 15c], a large shrub with many branches, small leaves and numerous white ‘tea-tree’ flowers.
Look to your left to see Eremaea pauciflora var. pauciflora [Section 15b], a small sprawling shrub with orange flowers.
Notice on your left Viola hederacea [Section 15a], a small mauve and white violet on a close groundcover.
Turn right, then right again to see on your right Verticordia galeata [Section 15f] with small bright yellow honey-scented flowers in profusion.
Turn left across the plank bridge to see in a pot on your left Olearia megalophylla [Section 15m].
Turn right down the hill to see on your right Leptospermum jingera [Section 15q], a large bush with drooping branches and white flowers that is endemic to Victoria.
On your right is Prostanthera hirtula [Section 15q], a white-flowered Mint Bush with small greyish leaves, found naturally in New South Wales and Victoria.
Go down the steps, then turn left up the other flight of steps to see on your right Eremophila bignoniiflora x polyclada [Section 15r].
On the right is Alyogyne ‘West Coast Gem’ [Section 15r], with clear purple ‘hibiscus’-type flowers which open for a short period only but are prolific.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Also on the right is Labichea lanceolata subsp. lanceolata [Section 15r], a large bush with bright green foliage and yellow flowers with a red throat.
Also on your right in a pot is Darwinia oxylepis [Section 15r], with dainty green foliage and pink bell-flowers.

intro: A walk along the Main Path this time of the year is a rewarding experience. Flowers are plentiful from the moment you leave the Visitor Information Centre (VIC).
p: On the left as you leave the VIC is a large specimen of Pandorea jasminoides [Section 212] covered in pink flowers and attractive mid-green foliage.
Actinotus helianthi ‘Starbright’ [Section 221], or Flannel Flower, is in a pot on the right as you leave the VIC.
Further along on the left in a pot is Anigozanthos ‘Bush Volcano’ [Section 210], a long-lasting kangaroo paw with red/orange flowers.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Homoranthus prolixus [Section 210] is also on the left in a pot.
Low on the right is the groundcover Pelargonium rodneyanum [Section 174], or Magenta Storksbill, with small bright pink/purple flowers on green lobed ‘geranium’ leaves.
Detour across the lawn from the café to see the outstanding small tree Melaleuca linariifolia ‘Seafoam’ [Section 243].
On the left in the small garden is Grevillea sericea [Section 244], with white spider flowers on an open airy bush.
On the left in the Ellis Rowan Garden is Callistemon ‘Little John’ [Section 131], a dwarf form of Callistemon viminalis.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Continue on the Main Path up the hill and look down to your left to see Baeckea astarteoides [Section 10], a small, delicate weeping bush with tiny pink flowers.
Further on your left is Leptospermum ‘Aphrodite’ [Section 10], with pink and green ‘tea-tree’ flowers on a large open bush with small light green foliage.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
On your left overhanging the path is a Callistemon species [Section 10], with pink flower spikes on a small weeping tree.
This is Leptospermum polygalifolium subsp. montanum [Section 9].
Further on your right is another large shrub, Kunzea ambigua [Section 9], covered in fluffy white blooms with a heavy honey scent.
Again on your right is Grevillea insignis subsp. insignis [Section 9], an open, rather straggly bush with blue-green prickly holly-like leaves.
The groundcover to your right is Persoonia chamaepitys [Section 27], or Creeping Geebung, with orange/gold flowers and light green foliage.

intro: We will walk to the new Asteraceae Garden today to see what is in flower. All plants are in Section 328.
fl: no [Section] refs found
p: As you enter the Asteraceae Garden on your right is Cassinia aureonitens or Yellow Cassinia with flat yellow composite heads of flower on a plant with linear foliage.
On your left is Senecio pinnatifolius var. pinnatifolius with yellow starbursts of flowers on grey divided foliage.
Brachyscome multifida ‘Breakoday’ is on your left with mauve flowers on small clumps of divided foliage.This cultivar is a popular daisy in many gardens.
In a pot on your right is Brachyscome segmentosa with mauve daisies with gold centres on a groundcover mat.
Brachyscome iberidifolia is in a pot on your right and is also scattered throughout the garden.
Also in a pot on your right is Brachyscome ‘Pacific Reef’ with bright pink daisies with gold centres on blue-green foliage.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Chrysocephalum apiculatum on your right has single gold flowerheads on a small bush.
Also on your right is Brachyscome rigidula with pale lilac flowers with gold centres.
On the left is Xerochrysum viscosum with bright yellow daisies on sticky green foliage.
On both the left and right is Leptorhynchos squamatus with bright gold terminal flowers on a small plant.
On the left is Rhodanthe chlorocephala subsp. rosea with many pink flowers fading to white with gold centres.
Also on the left is Schoenia filifolia subsp. subulifolia, also known as Showy Everlasting, with cheerful yellow daisies on thin stems.
On the right is Ammobium alatum with winged grey stems supporting white paper daisies with golden centres.
Rhodanthe anthemoides on the left is a long lasting white daisy on attractive clumps of grey foliage.
Brachyscome multifida ‘Alba’ on your left as you exit the garden is a small white daisy with gold centres.

intro: Take a shaded walk from the Visitors Information Centre (VIC) up the hill behind the café to see some festive flowers.
p: On the left across from the VIC is Rhododendron viriosum [Section 212], with magnificent coral bell flowers and shiny dark green leaves.
On your right in a pot is Blandfordia grandiflora [Section 221], or Christmas Bells,with large fluted red bell flowers tipped with yellow on thin stems above linear foliage.
Further along on your right in a pot is Swainsona formosa [Section 221] or Sturt’s Desert Pea with pale grey-green leaves and bright red pea flowers with shiny black centres or bosses.
On your right are several small trees of Banksia serrata [Section 174] or Saw Banksia behind the sculpture of Sir Joseph Banks.
Scaevola albida [Section 174] also on your right is a prostrate shrub native to southern Australia.
In a pot on your left is Anigozanthos ‘Bush Sunset’ [Section 210] with vibrant red Kangaroo Paw flowers on long stems.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Grevillea juncifolia [Section 210] on your left in a pot has with narrow grey bootlace leaves and long sprays of yellowish-white flowers.

Look up to see on your left Clerodendrum floribundum var. attenuatum [Section 125] or Lolly Bush, a small rainforest tree in full bloom with clusters of strongly scented white bell flowers against dark green foliage.
In a bed on your right is a dense groundcover, Grevillea ‘Poorinda Royal Mantle’ [Section 124], with masses of red toothbrush-like flowers that are a beacon for both birds and bees.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Further on your left is Hibiscus divaricatus [Section 114] with pure yellow flowers contrasting with maroon stamens on a straggly bush.
Also on the left, Hibiscus heterophyllus subsp. heterophyllus [Section 114] has many startlingly white flowers with deep red centres.
On the right is a bed filled with Kangaroo Paws, Anigozanthos flavidus [Section 17], in rusty orange and green shades.
On the left is a hybrid involving Hibiscus splendens [Section 114], with lolly-pink blooms with deeper-coloured throats.
Leptospermum subglabratum [Section 17], on the right, has masses of white tea-tree flowers on a weeping bush with small foliage.
Acmena smithii [Section 140], on your left, is a small tree with a dense crown of shiny green leaves covered in clusters of cream flowers.

intro: Take a walk from the Visitor Information Centre (VIC) along the Main Path to see some New Year’s flowers.
p: On the left across from the VIC look up to see Pandorea jasminoides [Section 212], a massive woody vine with plenty of pink bell flowers and shiny light green leaves.

On your right and left at the entrance to the VIC in pots is Blandfordia grandiflora [Section 221], or Christmas Bells,with large fluted red bell flowers tipped with yellow on thin stems above linear foliage.
Further along on your right is Spyridium burragorang [Section 174], with prominent white bracts and tiny central flowers.
Go across the bridge to see on your left Hibbertia patens [Section 131], showing off bright green foliage with yellow flowers.
Babingtonia pluriflora [Section 30] is covered in tiny white flowers that are often surrounded by a cloud of beetles.

Further on your right is Stenocarpus angustifolius [Section 30], a medium-sized bush with lance-shaped light green foliage in attractive contrast to lemon yellow clusters of flowers that are highly attractive to many insects.
Grevillea ‘LadyO’ [Section 24] on your left is a medium sized spreading shrub with red clusters of flowers on a neat bush.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Grevillea sericea [Section 26], or Silky Grevillea, is a shrub endemic to New South Wales.
On your right is Persoonia acerosa [Section 26], or Needle Geebung, with deep gold spiky flowers at the ends of bright green foliage.
Close to the Persoonia on your right is Grevillea ‘Canterbury Gold’ [Section 26], a hybrid between Grevillea victoriae and a prostrate form of G.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Also on your right is Adenanthos sericeus [Section 26], commonly known as Woolly Bush, a shrub native to the south coast of Western Australia.
Low on the right is Banksia petiolaris [Section 26], a ground-hugging banksia with yellowish cones.
As you enter the Sydney Basin on the left and right is Crowea exalata [Section 112], with pretty pink star flowers on soft foliage.
Banksia serrata [Section 112], or Saw Banksia, on the left has very large yellowish-green cones with grey tips.
Correa glabra var. glabra [Section 112] is around to your right, a large bush with many green tubular flowers.

intro: Take a walk today from the Visitors Information Centre (VIC) to the Rock Garden where there are plenty of interesting plants in flower.
p: On the left across from the VIC look up to see Pandorea jasminoides [Section 212], a massive woody vine with plenty of pink bell flowers and shiny light green leaves.
On the left of the entrance the VIC in a pot is Rhododendron viriosum [Section 221] with magnificent coral bell flowers on shiny dark green leaves.
Lythrum salicaria [Section 15v], or Purple Loosestrife, has terminal spikes of purple flowers which are very popular with bees.
Go up the stairs to see on your left Leptospermum deuense [Section 15c], with white ‘tea-tree’ flowers on a neat bush.
Further up the stairs on your right is Grevillea ‘Poorinda Royal Mantle’ [Section 15d], a vigorous groundcover with masses of red toothbrush flowers and persistent attention from the bees.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Also on your right is Chrysocephalum apiculatum [Section 15d], with bright gold button flowers on a grey green groundcover plant.
On your left and in many other places in the Rock Garden is Calostemma purpureum [Section 15b], or Garland Lily, with clusters of pink bell flowers on thin stems.
Calocephalus lacteus [Section 15b], or Milky Beauty-heads, is on your left with small white heads of flower on a grey green groundcover.
High on your left is Anigozanthos flavidus [Section 15h], a large clump of rusty red Kangaroo Paws.
On the rocks on your left is Muehlenbeckia axillaris [Section 15h], forming a wiry mat of tiny rounded leaves with masses of small yellow flowers.
Also on your left is Arthropodium milleflorum [Section 15h], commonly known as Vanilla Lily, with dainty pink vanilla-scented bell flowers on very thin stems.
High on the left is Acacia aneura var. aneura [Section 15l], commonly known as mulga, an open bush with gold balls of flowers on grey needle foliage.
On the left is Senecio linearifolius var. dangarensis [Section 15r], a tall grey-green shrub with yellow flower-heads.
Eremophila bignoniiflora × polyclada [Section 15r], on the left, is an open bush with green linear foliage and large mauve bell flowers, fading to white.
Hibbertia pedunculata [Section 15s], on the right, has tiny green foliage hugging the ground and showing off bright yellow flowers.

intro: We will visit the Red Centre Garden today. This garden has only been opened for just over a year and is still under development, being filled with plants that grow in the dry inland area of central Australia.
p: On the right after you leave the Visitor Information Center is Banksia victoriae [Section 174], or Woolly Orange Banksia, with a glorious orange felty cone on long linear toothed foliage.
Bear left up the hill behind the café to see on your right the huge white flowers of Crinum pedunculatum [Section 246], or Swamp Lily.
As you enter the Red Centre Garden on the left is Solanum sturtianum [Section 326], or Sturt’s Nightshade, with purple flowers with yellow anthers on an open bush of grey‑green foliage.
Bear left and on your right is Acacia kempeana [Section 326], also called Wichetty Bush, a small shrub with grey-green leaves and yellow rods of flowers.
On your left is Acacia rhodophloia [Section 326], a small upright tree with upward pointing linear foliage and thick yellow rods of flowers.
Dipteracanthus australasicus [Section 326], on the right, is a small plant with grey-green foliage and mauve tubular bell flowers, native to Western Australia.
Further on your right is Gossypium sturtianum [Section 326], or Sturt’s Desert Rose, the floral emblem of the Northern Territory.
Swainsona formosa [Section 326], or Sturt’s Desert Pea, on the left, is the iconic shiny red and black flower of central Australia.
Calotis erinacea [Section 326] on your right is a small shrub with bright yellow daisy flowers on fresh green foliage.
On your right is Sida calyxhymenia [Section 326], or Tall Sida, an erect grey leaved bush with small pale yellow cup flowers.
On the left are several bushes of Brachyscome iberidifolia [Section 326] or Swan River Daisy with ferny foliage and bright purple, almost iridescent flowers.
On your right is Rutidosis helichrysoides subsp. helichrysoides, or Grey Wrinklewort, with yellow pompom flowers on grey-green foliage.
Solanum orbiculatum subsp. orbiculatum on your left is a small, neat bush with purple “potato” flowers.
Further on your left is Calandrinia balonensis [Section 326], or Broad-leaf Parakeelya, a low bush of bright green succulent foliage with purple flowers on wiry maroon stems.
Eremophila willsii subsp. integrifolia [Section 326], or Sandhill Native Fuchsia, in a pot is a spindly shrub with mauve tubular flowers on green foliage.

intro: On the far left as you leave the Visitor Information Centre (VIC) is Correa alba [Section 221], or White Correa, a shrub with creamy-white bell flowers on dull green silver-backed foliage. In the wild it is found in coastal regions of south-eastern Australia.
p: On the far left as you leave the Visitor Information Centre (VIC) is Correa alba [Section 221], or White Correa, a shrub with creamy-white bell flowers on dull green silver-backed foliage.
On the near left as you leave the VIC in a pot is Pilidiostigma rhytispermum [Section 221], or Small-leaved Plum Myrtle, a medium woody shrub with small leaves and cream cup-shaped flowers.
On the right of the VIC, also in a pot, is Prostanthera densa [Section 221], or Villous Mintbush, a stiff, angular plant with pale green leaves and mauve flowers with orange markings.
Skirt in front of the café to see on your left Banksia ‘Stumpy Gold’ [Section 131], with fine, toothed linear foliage and short gold brush-like flower heads.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Further on your left is Epacris longiflora [Section 131], a prickly bush with red tubular flowers with white tips.
Correa ‘Summer Belle’ [Section 240], on the right, is a small plant with reddish bell flowers with green tips.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Callistemon viminalis [Section 310], on your right, is a medium-sized tree with drooping foliage and brilliant red brush-like flowers.
Turn up the hill to see on your left Eremophila oldfieldii subsp. angustifolia [Section 302], with fresh green linear foliage and bright salmon pink tubular bell flowers with prominent sepals.
Banksia spinulosa ‘Birthday Candles’ [Section 30], on your left, is coming into bloom with striking pale gold flower heads and bright green linear foliage.
On your right is Grevillea sericea [Section 26], with pink spider flowers on a long-flowering open bush.
On the right is Persoonia lanceolata [Section 26], a dense bush with small leaves and tiny yellow-gold flowers.
On your right is Banksia conferta subsp. penicillata [Section 26], or Newnes Plateau Banksia.
Grevillea manglesii subsp. manglesii [Section 24], or Birdsfoot Grevillea, is a large open bush with pincushion-like white flower heads all along the stems.
Further on your left is Adenanthos × cunninghamii [Section 24], with beautiful soft silver foliage and tiny red flowers.
Correa ‘Marian’s Marvel’ [Section 112], on your right, is a medium-sized dense bush with pale pink and green bell flowers.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)

intro: Start today’s walk from the Visitor Information Centre (VIC) and walk up the hill behind the café.
p: Spyridium burragorang [Section 174] on the right-hand side of the path has tiny white flowers surrounded by brown bracts and distinctive whitish floral leaves.
Also on the right in a pot is Hypocalymma jessicae [Section 174], a dainty bush with plenty of small pink flowers and heath-like foliage.
Veer left up the hill behind the café to see on your right a standard form of Grevillea bipinnatifida ‘Jingle Bells’ [Section 124].
Callistemon montanus [Section 104] is on the left with bright red brushes with gold tips.
Leptospermum amboinense [Section 104] is also on the left showing masses of small white “tea-tree” flowers on weeping foliage.
On your right is Chrysocephalum apiculatum [Section 17] with bright gold buttons on grey-green foliage.
On your left is Brachyscome graminea [Section 123], or Grass Daisy, a light green groundcover with white flower heads with gold centres.
At the top of the Rock Garden on the right is Grevillea ‘Mason’s Hybrid’ [Section 15h], a spreading bush with large spider blooms of pink, red and orange.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Also on the right is Grevillea lanigera [Section 15h], with grey-green foliage and pink and cream flowers on a low bush.
Xerochrysum bracteatum [Section 15h], or Paper Daisy, is on the right with a mass of bright gold papery flowerheads on green linear foliage.
On the right is Grevillea sericea subsp. sericea [Section 15k], an airy bush with light green foliage and white spider flowers.
Callistemon comboynensis [Section 15r], or Cliff Bottlebrush, is on your right with bright red flowers.
Also on your right is a low groundcover Commelina cyanea [Section 15r] with bright blue flowers.
On the left is Xerochrysum viscosum [Section 326], or Sticky Everlasting, a small yellow daisy with darker centres and tangled green foliage.
Also on the left in a pot is Xerochrysum bracteatum ‘Dargan Hill Monarch’ [Section 326], a magnificent pale yellow paper daisy with green foliage.

intro: Today we will concentrate on finding banksias in flower.
p: Banksia prionotes [Section 174] on the right-hand side in a pot is showing toothed grey-green foliage and white felty cones which develop a pale orange colour when mature.
On the left is Banksia ‘Stumpy Gold’ [Section 131], a neat low bush with fine, toothed linear foliage and short golden cones.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Also on your left is Banksia integrifolia [Section 131], a small tree with oblong green silver-backed leaves and greenish cones.
Banksia spinulosa var. collina [Section 131] on the left has fine linear foliage and slender, dull gold cones.

Veer left up the hill on the Main Path to see Banksia ericifolia subsp. ericifolia [Section 30] on your left, a long-flowering, medium-sized shrub with attractive divided foliage and long orange inflorescences.
On your right is Banksia heliantha [Section 30], which used to be known as Oak-leaved Dryandra before the reclassification of all dryandras to banksias.
On your left is Banksia spinulosa ‘Birthday Candles’ [Section 30], a dense bright green bush with attractive needle foliage and short yellow cones with rusty red styles.
‘Birthday Candles’ is a dwarf cultivar of Banksia spinulosa var. spinulosa developed by Bill Molyneux of Austraflora Nurseries in Montrose, Victoria.
On the right is Banksia spinulosa ‘Honeypots’ [Section 30], a small bush with fine-toothed foliage and chunky orange cones with red styles.
Also on the right is Banksia integrifolia subsp. integrifolia [Section 30], or Coast Banksia, a small tree with yellow cones with grey tips.
On the left is Banksia spinulosa var. neoanglica [Section 30], or New England Banksia, with silver-backed dark green foliage with yellow/gold cones held upright.
Banksia conferta var. pencillata [Section 25] or Newnes Plateau Banksia, also on the left, is a small tree covered in upward-pointing leaves.
Also on your right is Banksia spinulosa [Section 27], a medium-sized bush with large pale yellow cones held upright on toothed linear grey-green foliage.
On the left is Banksia ericifolia ‘Red Clusters’ [Section 25], with heath-like foliage and very large red cones.
Turn left back along the road to see on your right Banksia aemula [Section 24], or Wallum Banksia, a small gnarled tree with knobby bark and very large squat green cones.

intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Information Centre (VIC) towards the Sydney Region Gully.
p: Swainsona formosa [Section 221] is on the right-hand side in a pot as you leave the VIC.
Also in a pot on the right is Prostanthera densa [Section 221], or Villous Mintbush, a stiff, angular plant with pale green leaves and mauve flowers with orange markings.
On your left is Grevillea bipinnatifida ‘Jingle Bells’ [Section 124].
Just before you cross the paved road directly ahead and move onto the dirt path, on your right is Callistemon subulatus [Section 10].
Continue on the dirt path to see Callistemon citrinus [Section 9] on your left, a long-flowering shrub with bright red brush-like flowers.
Further on your left is Banksia paludosa [Section 28], with plain gold cones.
Also on your left is Lambertia formosa [Section 28], or Mountain Devil, with red flowers with long styles and bracts.

As you turn left up the hill on the paved road on your left is Banksia integrifolia subsp. compar [Section 28], or Coast Banksia, a small tree with long yellow cones and dark green leaves with silver backs.
Telopea mongaensis [Section 28], or Monga Waratah on your left, has bright red flowerheads held upright above an open bush of dull green foliage.
On the right is Correa ‘Canberra Bells’ [Section 112], a small neat bush with red and white bell flowers.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Banksia aemula [Section 191g], or Wallum Banksia, on your right, is a small gnarled tree with knobby bark and large squat green cones.
Banksia ericifolia [Section 191g] on the right has squat yellow cones with rusty red styles.
Also on your right is Banksia spinulosa var. cunninghamii [Section 191g], a small tree with dull gold flowers with black styles.
Behind the Sydney Region Gully sign on your right is Melaleuca thymifolia [Section 191l], a small bush with close blue-green foliage and purple ‘claw’ flowers.

intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Information Centre (VIC) to the Rock Garden.
p: Platytheca galioides [Section 221] is on the left-hand side in a pot as you leave the VIC.
Further along in a pot on the right is Banksia prionotes [Section 174], commonly known as Acorn Banksia or Orange Banksia, which has toothed linear foliage and orange cones with a felty texture.
On your left is Prostanthera phylicifolia [Section 210], or Spiked Mint-bush, which has masses of small mauve flowers on a lax bush which scrambles down a bank.
Bear left up the hill behind the café to see on your left Acronychia littoralis [Section 114].
On your left is Banksia aemula [Section 15c], or Wallum Banksia, a small gnarled tree with knobby bark and large squat green cones.
Just before you reach the entrance to the Rock Garden, on your left is Hibbertia scandens [Section 15c], or Snake Vine.
Just after you enter the Rock Garden and go up the steps, on your right is Lomatia tinctoria [Section 15d] with sprays of scented white curled flowers on upright divided foliage.
Further on your left is Banksia integrifolia subsp. integrifolia [Section 15c], or Coast Banksia, a vigorous mound of foliage and flowers.
On your right is Correa ‘Ivory Bells’[Section 15d], with creamy bell flowers on darker green silver-backed foliage.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Also on your right is Banksia spinulosa ‘Honeypots’ [Section 15d], a medium-sized bush with fine, upright toothed foliage and many golden cones.
Chrysocephalum apiculatum [Section 15d], low down on your right, has bright golden-orange button flowers on grey-green foliage.
On your left in a pot is Acacia pterocaulon [Section 15e], with large gold balls of flowers on long flattened stems.
Grevillea manglesii [Section 15d], or Birdsfoot Grevillea, on your right, is a large bush with frothy white terminal clusters of flowers and tripartite ‘birdsfoot’ foliage.
Cross the plank bridge to see high on your left Acacia aneura var. aneura [Section 15l], or Mulga, with fine grey-green needle foliage and short rods of yellow flowers.
Also on your left is an attractive clump of Banksia spinulosa ‘Birthday Candles’[Section 15l], forming a mound of green linear foliage with masses of golden cones with rusty red styles.

intro: Today we will visit the Red Centre Garden, which is a relatively new area specialising in the flora of the dry inland of Australia. All plants, except where otherwise noted, are in Section 326.
p: As you enter the Red Centre Garden on the left is Solanum sturtianum, or Sturt’s Nightshade, with purple flowers with yellow anthers on an open bush of grey-green foliage.
Bear left up the hill and on your right is Acacia kempeana, also called Wichetty Bush, a small dense shrub with grey-green leaves and short yellow rods of flowers.
On your left is Acacia rhodophloia, a vase-shaped bush with plenty of upward-pointing linear foliage and thick yellow rods of flowers.
Further on your right is Gossypium sturtianum, or Sturt’s Desert Rose, the floral emblem of the Northern Territory.
Swainsona formosa, or Sturt’s Desert Pea, on the left, has shiny red and black flowers.
Calotis erinacea,on your right, is a small shrub with bright yellow daisy flowers and fresh green foliage.
Also closer on your right is Sida calyxhymenia, or Tall Sida, a sparse grey-leaved bush with small pale yellow cup flowers.
On the left is Acacia ammobia, or Mount Connor Wattle, a large shrub with leathery, grey-green linear foliage and large golden rods of flowers.
On the right is Ptilotus obovatus, or Silvertails, a short bush with grey foliage and pink-tipped white flower heads.
On both your right and left is Rutidosis helichrysoides subsp. helichrysoides, or GreyWrinklewort, with yellow button flowers ongrey-green foliage.
Solanum orbiculatum subsp. orbiculatum on your left is a small, neat bush with purple“potato” flowers and rounded silvery-green foliage.
Further on your left is Calandrinia balonensis, or Broad-leaf Parakeelya, a low bush of bright green succulent foliage with purple flowers on wiry maroon stems.
Keep walking left towards the greenhouses and Telopea speciosissima × oreades [Section 191t], is on your right over the wall.
On your left is a small weeping bush, Callistemon viminalis ‘Rose Opal’ [Section 87], with rose pink bottlebrush flowers.
Also on your left is a small tree, Callistemon ‘Peak Downs’ [Section 87], with bright red gold-tipped bottlebrush flowers.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)

intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Information Centre (VIC) behind the café and along the bitumen road at the top of the Rock Garden.
p: Bear left up the hill behind the café to see on your right Grevillea bipinnatifida ‘Jingle Bells’ [Section 124], a standard grevillea with deeply-divided stiff, prickly foliage and many trusses of pink and orange flowers.

Further along on the right is Banksia spinulosa var. spinulosa [Section 109], or Hairpin Banksia, which is found in open forests and woodlands of the coasts and mountains of New South Wales and Queensland.
On your left is Notelaea lloydii [Section 114].
On your left are several plants of Plectranthus alloplectus [Section 114], with coarse ovate foliage and long sprays of mauve flowers.
On your right is Epacris calvertiana var. calvertiana [Section 17], which occurs in coastal regions of New South Wales, with cream bell flowers on dark green foliage.
Turn right along the road to see on your right Chamelaucium ‘Cascade Brook’ [Section 17], or Geraldton Wax.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Chamelaucium uncinatum ‘Murfit Rose’ [Section 17] on your right is another Geraldton Wax cultivar, with fine foliage and paler pink flowers that darken as they age.
Further on your right is Grevillea lanigera [Section 15h], with grey-green foliage and pink and cream flowers on a low shrub.
On your right a little down the path under the “Genus Hakea” sign is Hakea drupacea [Section 20], commonly known as Sweet Hakea.
Hakea varia [Section 20], on your right, has hard prickly variable foliage which droops and small white starburst flowers.
Also on your right is Grevillea triloba [Section 22], a spreading shrub with grey-green foliage and white starburst flowers.
Correa reflexa var. speciosa [Section 112], on your right occurs in coastal New South Wales and Victoria.
Turn right down the Main Path to see on your left Correa ‘Marian’s Marvel’ [Section 112], with flared pale pink bell flowers with long greenish tips.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Grevillea centristigma [Section 26], also on your left, is a small bush with soft lush foliage fringed with with white hairs.

intro: Today we will walk from the Visitors Information Centre (VIC) along the Main Path.
p: Notice on your right in a pot Astroloma foliosum [Section 174], commonly known as Candle Cranberry, a small shrub species which is endemic to the Perth region in Western Australia.
Further along on the left is Isopogon ‘Little Drumsticks’ [Section 210], a low bushy shrub with well-displayed yellow flower-heads.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
On your left at the start of the bridge is Olearia argophylla [Section 305], or Native Musk.
On your left is Banksia ‘Stumpy Gold’ [Section 131], with finely-toothed linear foliage and masses of short gold flower-heads with rusty red styles.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
On your left is Eucalyptus gregsoniana [Section 131], with a grey trunk and white fluffy flowers.
On your right Acacia alata var. biglandulosa [Section 240], or Winged Wattle, has flattened phyllodes and masses of white fluffy balls of flowers.
Grevillea saccata [Section 30] in a pot on your left has weeping branches and pinkish-orange flowers.
On your left behind the pot is Grevillea diminuta [Section 30], with dark green foliage and rusty red bunches of flowers.
On your right is a pink-flowered form of Correa alba [Section 30], a small upright bush with grey-green foliage.
On your left is Banksia spinulosa var. neoanglica [Section 25], or New England Banksia, with silver-backed dark green foliage with yellow/gold upright flower heads.
Banksia spinulosa var. spinulosa [Section 27], on your right, is found in open forests and woodlands of the coasts and mountains of New South Wales and Queensland.
On your left is Banksia ericifolia ‘Red Clusters’ [Section 25], a small tree with green heath-like foliage and very large orange-red cones.
Banksia spinulosa var. collina [Section 27], on your right a little further down the gravel path, has fine linear foliage and slender, dull gold cones.
On your right is Buckinghamia celsissima [Section 27], or Ivory Curl, a small tree with fragrant dense terminal clusters of ivory flowers.
Cross the road to see on your left Hakea cycloptera [Section 24], or Elm-seed Hakea, a small bush with thin spiky grey foliage and many curled pink blooms at the base of the leaves.

intro: Today we will walk from the Visitor Information Centre (VIC) up the hill to the Acacia section.
p: On your right in a pot is Banksia calophylla [Section 174,] with stiff, toothed grey-green foliage and small reddish-orange flower-heads hidden amongst the foliage.
Further along on the right is Epacris reclinata [Section 174], with clusters of small white tubular flowers on wiry foliage.
Also on your right is Epacris impressa [Section 174], a straggly bush with bright pink tubular flowers.
Still on the right is yet another species of Epacris, Epacris longiflora [Section 174].
On your left is Prostanthera phylicifolia [Section 210], or Spiked Mint-bush, which has masses of small mauve flowers on a loose shrub which is scrambling down a bank.
On your right is Thryptomene denticulata [Section 174], with arching stems bearing close grey-green foliage and pink flowers.
On the right is Chamelaucium ‘Cascade Jewel’ [Section 174], a cultivar of Geraldton Wax.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
On your right is Calothamnus tuberosus [Section 14], a stiff upright bush with spiky grey-green linear foliage.
Also on the right is Eremophila oppositifolia [Section 14], a sparse bush with grey foliage and pinkish-white tubular bell flowers.
Turn left towards the Red Centre Garden to see on your left Acacia oshanesii [Section 3], which is native to coastal New South Wales and Queensland.
On your right is Acacia falcata [Section 18], or Sickle Wattle, which is native to eastern Australia.
Acacia terminalis [Section 18], further along on your right, is a small tree whose range extends through New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania.
Turn right down the Main Path to see on both your left and right Acacia subulata, [Section 18], or Awl Leaf Wattle.
Podolobium aciculiferum [Section 18] is on your left with golden pea flowers and sharply pointed dark green foliage.
On your right is Acacia consobrina [Section 18], a native of southwestern Western Australia.

intro: Between the two entrances to the Rock Garden on your right is Guichenotia ledifolia [Section 4], with grey-green foliage covered in masses of dusty pink five-petalled flowers with maroon centres. It is native to south western Western Australia.
p: Between the two entrances to the Rock Garden on your right is Guichenotia ledifolia [Section 4], with grey-green foliage covered in masses of dusty pink five-petalled flowers with maroon centres.
Go through the right-hand entrance to see on the left Correa pulchella ‘Pink Mist’ [Section 15s], with dainty pink bell flowers on a small bush.
Also on your left is Banksia fraseri var. fraseri [Section 15p], a small shrub with finely divided foliage and small, domed brown-gold cones.
Turn right to see on the left Leucopogon neoanglicus [Section 15k] with dark red, fine-leaved foliage and pink tubular bell flowers.
Also on your left is Zieria adenophora [Section 15k], with dark red foliage and small white flowers.
On your left is Banksia spinulosa ‘Birthday Candles’ [Section 15l], a dense bush with attractive needle foliage and short yellow cones with rusty red styles.
Also on the left is Banksia integrifolia subsp. integrifolia [Section 15l], or Coast Banksia, a vigorous mound of foliage and flowers.
Turn left and continue straight ahead to see on your left Banksia ‘Cape Patterson Dwarf’ [Section 15q], a small bush with silver-backed, dark green foliage and lime-yellow cones.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
On the left is Eremophila subfloccosa subsp. subfloccosa [Section 15d], a low spreading shrub with furry silver foliage clasping the stem and green tubular flowers.
Also on your left is Chorizema cordatum [Section 15d], or Heart-leaved Flame Pea, a showy plant with vivid orange/red flowers on a weeping shrub with bright green prickly foliage.
On your right is Homoranthus darwinioides [Section 15f], with dark purple-grey foliage and pendulous white flowers that turn reddish with age.

Bear left down the hill to see on your left Grevillea manglesii subsp. ornithopoda [Section 15d], or Birdsfoot Grevillea, a large open shrub with white pincushion-like flowerheads all along the stems.
Banksia spinulosa ‘Honeypots’ [Section 15d], also on the left , is a medium-sized bush with fine, upright toothed foliage and many gold cones.
Correa ‘Ivory Bells’ [Section 15d], is on your left with creamy bell flowers and dark green silver-backed leaves.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
On your right is Grevillea lanigera [Section 15c] with grey-green foliage and pink and cream flowers on a low bush.

intro: On your right, in a pot, is Astroloma foliosum [Section 174]. Commonly known as Candle Cranberry, it is a small shrub species endemic to the Perth region in Western Australia. This plant has very fine foliage and upright red “firecracker” tubular flowers with black and yellow tips.
p: On your right, in a pot, is Astroloma foliosum [Section 174].
Cross the bridge and skirt past the café to see on the left Banksia ‘Stumpy Gold’ [Section 131], with fine, toothed linear foliage and short gold cones.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Also on your left is Eucalyptus gregsoniana [Section 131], a mallee (multi-stemmed tree) with grey trunks and white fluffy flowers.
On your right is Acacia alata var. biglandulosa [Section 240], or Winged Wattle.
On your left is Banksia spinulosa var. collina [Section 131], with fine linear foliage and slender, dull gold cones.
Go up the hill, bear right and on your left is Banksia ericifolia subsp. ericifolia [Section 30], a long-flowering medium-sized shrub with attractive feathery foliage and long orange cones.
Also on the left in a pot is Grevillea saccata [Section 30], with terminal clusters of reddish-orange flowers.
Also on the left and behind the pot is Grevillea diminuta [Section 30], with dark green foliage and rusty red clusters of flowers.
On your right is Grevillea acropogon [Section 30], a low bush with green foliage and deep red flower-clusters.
On your left is Adenanthos cygnorum [Section 30], a small bush with grey-green silky foliage and red spidery flowers.
Also on your left is Banksia spinulosa var. neoanglica [Section 30], or New England Banksia, with silver-backed dark green foliage with upright yellow/gold cones.
On your right is Banksia ‘Cape Patterson Dwarf’ [Section 26], a small bush with dark green silver-backed foliage and lime-yellow cones.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
On your left is Grevillea manglesii subsp. ornithopoda [Section 24], or Birdsfoot Grevillea, a large open bush with pincushion-like white flowerheads all along the stems.

Grevillea tripartita subsp. macrostylis [Section 26], on the right, is an open, rangy plant with dark green, prickly, three-lobed foliage and large single red and cream flowers with long showy red styles.
Grevillea dielsiana [Section 26], also on your right, has intricate prickly linear foliage and large yellow/orange flowers with red styles.

intro: Today’s walk is along the main path to explore the Banks Loop.
p: Outside the Visitor Information Centre is Banksia calophylla [Section 174].
On the right as you walk along the Main Path is Darwinia macrostegia [Section 174].
In a pot on the right is Leucopogon attenuatus [Section 174], a small shrub with tiny white flowers.
Also on your right is Epacris impressa [Section 174], a straggly bush with bright pink tubular flowers that have indentations at the base.
At the end of Banks Walk on your right is Chamelaucium ‘Cascade Jewel ’[Section 174].
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Walk on past the café and on your left is Eucalyptus gregsoniana [Section 131], with a grey trunk and white fluffy flowers.
Also on your left is Epacris longiflora [Section 131], with thin tubular red and white flowers on a light green bush.
On your left is Homoranthus flavescens [Section 143], with silver to blue-grey leaves on spreading horizontal branches.
Adjacent is Pimelea latifolia [Section 143], with unobtrusive white flowers.
On your right is Banksia ‘Giant Candles’ [Section 310], a large shrub that can grow up to five metres.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Further along on your left is Grevillea floribunda [Section 143], a small shrub with attractive light green and yellow flowers.

Continue on in a clockwise direction around the loop and you will find a group of banksias on your left with contrasting foliage, flower colour and growth habit, including Banksia spinulosa [Section 306].
On your left is Acacia podalyrifolia [Section 126], a tall silver-grey shrub or small tree also known as the Queensland Silver Wattle.
As you turn the corner there are a number of plants of Grevillea ‘Rosy Posy’ [Section 128].
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Adjacent is Acacia siculiformis [Section 128], an erect prickly shrub with the common name of Dagger Wattle.

intro: Today we will walk along the Main Path to see the winter-flowering banksias and grevilleas.
p: Cross the bridge and skirt past the café to see on your left Correa bauerlenii [Section 244] with long green bell flowers and shiny foliage.
Further on the left is Banksia ‘Stumpy Gold’ [Section 131], with fine, toothed linear foliage and short gold flowering cones.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Also on your left is Banksia spinulosa var. collina [Section 131], with fine linear foliage and slender, dull gold cones.
Turn left up the hill and continue along the path to see on the right Grevillea acropogon [Section 30], a low bush with green foliage and deep red clusters of flower.
On your left is Banksia spinulosa var. neoanglica [Section 25], or New England Banksia, with silver-backed dark green foliage with yellow/gold upright cones.
Also on your left is Grevillea rhyolitica subsp. rhyolitica [Section 25], or Deua Grevillea, endemic to the south coast of New South Wales.
On the right [Section 26] and also on your left [Section 24] is Grevillea ‘Lady O’.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
On your right is Banksia ‘Cape Patterson Dwarf’ [Section 26], a small bush with silver-backed dark green foliage and lime-yellow cones.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
Further on your right is Grevillea lavandulacea [Section 26], commonly known as Lavender Grevillea, endemic to south-eastern South Australia and western and central Victoria.
Again on your right is Grevillea centristigma [Section 26], a small bush with soft lush foliage fringed with white hairs.

On your right behind the seat is Grevillea tripartita subsp. macrostylis [Section 26], an open, rangy plant with dark green, prickly, three-lobed foliage and large single red and cream flowers with long showy red styles.
Still on your right low down is Isopogon asper [Section 26], a shrub that is endemic to the southwest botanical province of Western Australia, first described by botanist Robert Brown in 1830.
Grevillea ripicola [Section 24], on the left, commonly known as Collie Grevillea, is a shrub endemic to south-west Western Australia.
On your right is a member of the Grevillea haplantha group [Section 26], a spindly bush with linear foliage and large red spider flowers with long styles.
Grevillea wilsonii x tripartita [Section 26], is on your right, a tall, rangy bush with prickly foliage and large pink spider flowers with red styles.

intro: This week it is time to focus on our wonderful wattles.
p: Just before the bridge to the café see on your right Acacia myrtifolia [Section 174], an interesting and unusual wattle that has bright red new growth and stems with green elliptical phyllodes (modified leaf-stems) and cream balls of flowers.
Further on the right is Acacia siculiformis [Section 128], a very stiff, upright shrub with pointed, dark green phyllodes and cream balls of flowers.
Bear right to see on your right Acacia podalyriifolia [Section 126], or Queensland Silver Wattle, with large golden balls of flowers and attractive grey-green foliage.
Turn left up the hill and continue along the path to see on the left Leucopogon melaleucoides [Section 110] or Snowbush, a small compact shrub with dark green foliage and white clusters of flowers.
Turn left up the steps to see Acacia amoena [Section 3], or Boomerang Wattle, on your left.
Further up the hill on your left is Acacia covenyi [Section 3], commonly known as Blue Bush.
Across the road on your right is Acacia parvipinnula [Section 18], or Silver-stemmed Wattle, which is a tree with dark green ferny foliage and pale yellow balls of flower.
Further on your left is Acacia oshanesii [Section 3], native to coastal New South Wales and Queensland.
Again on your left is Acacia caesiella [Section 3], from the central slopes of New South Wales.

Bear right along the edge of the Eucalypt Lawn to see on your right Acacia cardiophylla [Section 18], or West Wyalong Wattle, with ferny, light green bipinnate foliage and masses of yellow balls of flower.
Still on your right is Acacia parvifolia [Section 18], with soft grey fringed foliage and pale yellow balls of flowers.
Acacia baileyana [Section 18], on the left , commonly known as Cootamundra Wattle, is a shrub native to southern New South Wales.
On your left is Acacia boormanii [Section 18] or Snowy River Wattle with fine needle foliage and masses of golden ball flowers.
Acacia consobrina [Section 18], is on your left, native to southwestern Western Australia.
Acacia venulosa [Section 18] is further along on your left with green linear foliage and bright yellow balls of flowers.

intro: We will focus again on wattles in bloom. The car park provides a variety of species to enjoy.
p: Turn left as you exit the Visitor Information Centre, then left down the hill to see on your right Acacia obliquinervia [Section 225].
On your left is Acacia pycnantha [Section 224], or Golden Wattle, the floral emblem of Australia (pictured above).
Further on your left is a clump of Acacia dawsonii [Section 224], or Poverty Wattle, medium-sized bushes with grey-green foliage covered in small yellow balls of flowers.
At the top of the steps on your right is the groundcover Acacia cultriformis ‘Cascade’ [Section 226], dropping over the wall in a fall of triangular green foliage and yellow balls of flowers.
Bear right across the carpark to see on your left Acacia cardiophylla [Section 227], with divided feathery foliage and masses of small yellow flower balls.
Also on your left is a prostrate form of Acacia baileyana [Section 227], or Cootamundra Wattle, with fringed grey-green foliage and yellow racemes of flowers.
Further on your left is Acacia havilandiorum [Section 227], a small bush with grey-green needle foliage and gold ball flowers.
Bear left with care down the road to see on your right Acacia buxifolia [Section 225], or Box-leaf Wattle, an open bush with red stems, small grey-green foliage and golden flowers.
Turn left into the carpark to see on your right Acacia williamsonii [Section 228], with yellow-green linear foliage and yellow balls of flowers.
Further on your right is Acacia hakeoides [Section 228], or Hakea Wattle, a small tree with linear green foliage, reddish stems, and clusters of large yellow flower balls.

Go down the steps, turn right along the footpath, and cross the car park to see in the far right-hand corner Acacia decurrens [Section 116], a tree with finely-divided green foliage and yellow balls of flowers.

Further on your right is Acacia subulata [Section 116], or Awl-leaf Wattle, a small tree with dark-green needle foliage and drooping clusters of pale yellow flower balls which open sequentially towards the tip.
Also on your right is Acacia buxifolia subsp. buxifolia [Section 116], a small bush with grey-green foliage and gold ball flowers.
On your right is Acacia genistifolia [Section 175], with spiky dark-green foliage and masses of cream ball flowers.
Bear right along the boardwalk and left around the corner to see across the road Acacia filicifolia [Section 169], or Fern-leaf Wattle.

intro: We will take a short walk along the Main Path today, where there are plenty of plants in flower.
p: Turn right as you exit the Visitor Information Centre (VIC) to see on your right Platytheca galioides [Section 221], with fine green foliage and deep purple bell flowers.
Also on your right is Grevillea rosmarinifolia ‘Scarlet Sprite’ [Section 174] with fine green linear foliage and red spider flowers.
Further on your right is Acacia gordonii [Section 174], a small shrub with fine, close dark green foliage and bright golden balls of flowers.
Chorizema cordatum [Section 174], or Heart-leaved Flame Pea, on the right in a pot is a showy plant with vivid red flowers on a weeping shrub with bright green prickly foliage.
On the right in a pot is Hovea asperifolia [Section 174], with grey-green linear foliage close to the stem and small purple flowers with darker centres.
Acacia myrtifolia [Section 174] is an interesting and unusual wattle that has bright red new growth and stems with green elliptical phyllodes and cream balls of flowers.
Cross the bridge and skirt past the café to see on your left Daviesia horrida [Section 245], with grey spiky linear foliage, yellow buds and small pea flowers of orange and red.
Further on your left is Grevillea sericea subsp. sericea [Section 244], a small bush with light green foliage and white fluffy flowers.
Also on your left is Libertia paniculata [Section 244], with light green strappy foliage and small white flowers held high.
Epacris longifolia [Section 131], or Native Fuchsia, on your left has thin tubular red flowers with white tips on a small prickly bush.
Further on your right is Phebalium squamulosum subsp. lineare [Section 240], a medium shrub with dull green foliage and yellow star flowers.
Grevillea rhyolitica subsp. rhyolitica, or Deua Flame [Section 240], on your right is a large bush with dark green foliage and bright red spider flowers.

Turn right towards the Crosbie Morrison Building to see on your right Hibbertia empetrifolia [Section 240], a groundcover with small green leaves and wiry stems ending in yellow flowers, from south-eastern New South Wales.
Turn right again towards the VIC to see on your left the Wee Jasper Grevillea, Grevillea iaspicula [Section 240], with bright green linear foliage and pink/cream flowers.
On your left is Philotheca myoporoides [Section 240], a neat bush with dull green foliage, pink buds and white star flowers endemic to south-eastern Australia.

intro: We will walk to the waterfall today, seeing plenty of flowering plants along the way.
p: Turn right as you exit the Visitor Information Centre (VIC) to see on your right in a pot Telopea ‘Essie’s Gift’, with long green leaves and spectacular dark pink flowers.
no species name printed (genus and cultivar only)
